Title: How primary health care teams perceive the integration of oral health care into their practice: A qualitative study
Snippet: Following a thematic content analysis, four phases of qualitative analysis were identified as detailed by Bengtsson [23]: 1) decontextualization; 2) recontextualization; 3) categorization; and 4) compilation. Each of these stages was revised by other research team members who had deep knowledge on the integration concept in different disciplines. The involvement of an interdisciplinary research team prevented errors in data analysis, personal and interpretation bias, and ensured that no relevant data were excluded, thereby maintaining the confirmability and the credibility of the analysis [25]. 

In the phase of decontextualization, transcription of data was performed with repeated examination of recorded data by the first author (HH). Debriefing and reflexive field notes made it possible to better understand the context and the participants' discourse. Then, an "inductive open coding process" followed [26]. The content areas were identified and accordingly, the text was divided into meaning units, which were subsequently condensed and transformed into codes. The use of a code explanation document facilitated the tracking of coding decisions, and maximized the dependability of the data analysis. 

In the recontextualization phase, codes were reviewed against the original interview transcriptions. The research team regularly and thoroughly discussed uncertainties in coding and interpretation, and obtained agreement to ensure the study's credibility. 

In the phase of categorization, codes with similar conceptual content (meaning units) were grouped to identify the themes (Table 1). 

Finally, the last stage (compilation) comprised analysis and interpretation. Although descriptive, the manifest analysis was followed by a latent analysis to understand hidden meanings of the original texts. 

In the data interpretation, similarities and differences in rural and urban settings as well as the literature findings were considered, to maximize the transferability and authenticity of the research. Trustworthiness of the study was maximized by using principal guidelines in qualitative research [26]. A respondent validation was performed with 5 individuals. 

Data analysis was conducted manually and was assisted by the use of Atlas-ti software (ATLAS-ti Scientific Software Development GmbH, Berlin, Germany). Consolidated criteria for reporting qualitative research (COREQ) were followed.

Title: What knowledge and skills are needed for community volunteers to take on a signposting role in community-based palliative care? A qualitative study
Snippet: This qualitative research is driven by a social constructivist epistemology, recognizing the impact of contextual factors on interpersonal actions, viewing reality as dynamic and socially constructed, and interpreting human realities as shared and co-constructed meanings. Inductive qualitative thematic analysis was chosen to analyze the data because there is little literature on the research topic. 24,25 The following iterative coding methods were used: (1) familiarization of data, (2) generating initial codes, (3) combining codes into themes, (4) reviewing themes, (5) determining the significance of themes, and (6) reporting of findings. 24 The analysis began with reading the transcripts by two authors (S.V.S., S.V.) to gain a global understanding of the content of the data. The data were coded by S.V.S. and S.V. and the coding framework was discussed on various occasions (weekly meetings between S.V.S. and S.V., and project group meetings every 6 weeks) and validated by all other authors. 5][26] Both coders independently conducted a primary analysis of five transcripts (generating initial codes) and compared them with each other. S.V.S. then combined codes into themes. 5][26] SVS established relationships between the different codes to establish an overarching conceptual scheme with provisional themes and subthemes, which was discussed, reviewed, and validated by the authors (S.V., K.C., L.D., and S.D.). The final agreed-upon coding scheme was then applied to all transcripts. S.V.S. and S.V. independently used the conceptual coding scheme on the same interview transcripts to check for the validity and coherence of the codes and themes. The conceptual coding scheme was tested as such for multiple transcripts and adjusted where necessary by the project group until the researchers arrived at a coding scheme that represented each coder's insights and was considered valid by the project group. Finally, this coding scheme was applied to the transcripts in a final coding round. The coding scheme (including main themes and subthemes) and associated quotes were structured into a table and used to create our final analysis.

Title: Interpreting the Choice Logic Surrounding High-Scoring Students’ Enrollment in China’s Vocational Secondary–Undergraduate Articulation Program: A Theoretical Thematic Analysis of Public Discourse
Snippet: Thematic analysis (TA) is now widely used in qualitative research. Recent methodological scholarship has stressed that TA should not be regarded as a single, standardized analytic technique, but rather as a family of methods that differ in their philosophical assumptions, analytic procedures, and conceptualisations of themes (Braun & Clarke, 2022). https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16050734 

In contrast to purely inductive forms of thematic analysis, theoretical thematic analysis refers to an approach to thematic analysis in which researchers draw on an established theoretical framework, research perspective, or predefined analytical dimensions as the point of departure, and employ a top-down strategy to code qualitative data, identify themes, and interpret meanings (Braun & Clarke, 2006). Rational choice theory provided the initial analytical framework, while close engagement with the empirical materials allowed the coding scheme and themes to be continuously revised and refined. 

All discourse materials were imported into NVivo 15.0 for systematic coding. Deductively, four top-level analytical dimensions were constructed around action foundations, action purposes, action consequences, and institutional-cultural influences. Inductive coding was used to refine initial codes and subthemes within these predefined analytical dimensions. For example, initial codes such as "academic performance" and "personal traits" were identified through repeated engagement with the data and further compared during later stages of analysis. Table 2 provides illustrative examples of this coding process. Second-cycle coding was conducted to compare, merge, and reorganize the initial codes into more analytical subthemes. For instance, codes such as "academic performance" and "personal traits" were integrated into the subtheme of "individual competence". The coding system's saturation was carefully tested. As the number of analyzed texts increased, the emergence of new conceptual categories gradually declined. By the time the 14th text was coded, the coding outcomes had stabilized. Considering the potential volatility of saturation, an additional four interactive discourse samples were coded. The extracted conceptual elements showed a high degree of overlap with the existing coding scheme, and no new categories emerged. Potentially identifying personal details were removed, minimized, or replaced with generic descriptors where appropriate.

Title: Identifying essential implementation strategies: a mixed methods process evaluation of a multi-strategy policy implementation intervention for schools
Snippet: Interviews were audio-recorded and transcribed verbatim. Interview facilitators checked transcripts for accuracy, corrected as necessary and anonymised any identifiable comments. The final copies were entered into QSR NVivo [35] for inductive thematic analysis using the standard approach reported by Braun and Clarke [36]. First, two experienced members of the research team (i) independently coded a subset of transcripts, (ii) checked for agreeance and resolved discrepancies with a third researcher, and (iii) developed a combined code scheme. 

Fig. 1 An overview of the convergent mixed method analytic procedure used for this study, including method of data collection and analysis to address each research objective. Quantitative data collection measures and method of analysis for research objective A is displayed on the left. Qualitative data collection measures and method of analysis for research objective B is displayed on the right. Both sides converge for the mixed methods procedure and interpretation for research objective C 

One of the researchers then applied the code scheme to the remaining transcripts, discussing new codes with the other researcher and updating where necessary. The analysis pair then looked for patterns within the final codes and generated a list of themes that emerged in relation to research objective B. The proposed list of themes was reviewed, modified where required and finalised with names and definitions for each. This process was guided by a consensual qualitative research process [37] inclusive of ongoing discourse and confirmation with other members of the PACE evaluation and delivery team. In addition, one member of the research team searched project officer transcripts and recorded for each, the top three strategies reported as essential for successful program implementation (research objective C).

Title: Design and Control Issues in Qualitative Case Study Research
Snippet: Recent interest in qualitative research methodology has created opportunities to explore conceptual relationships between qualitative and quantitative design and methods. Though it is accepted by some researchers that theory development may be achieved by qualitative case study research, these examples are rare. A qualitative case study, which blended notions of experimental method with qualitative research, has been described and the design rationale examined. By rendering more explicit the arguments and decision making processes that contribute to qualitative case study design, it is possible to gain a clearer assessment of a study's strengths and limitations, as well as contribute to our understanding of qualitative case study design and methodology.

Thematic analysis (TA) is now widely used in qualitative research. Recent methodological scholarship has stressed that TA should not be regarded as a single, standardized analytic technique, but rather as a family of methods that differ in their philosophical assumptions, analytic procedures, and conceptualisations of themes (Braun & Clarke, 2022). https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16050734 

In contrast to purely inductive forms of thematic analysis, theoretical thematic analysis refers to an approach to thematic analysis in which researchers draw on an established theoretical framework, research perspective, or predefined analytical dimensions as the point of departure, and employ a top-down strategy to code qualitative data, identify themes, and interpret meanings (Braun & Clarke, 2006). Rational choice theory provided the initial analytical framework, while close engagement with the empirical materials allowed the coding scheme and themes to be continuously revised and refined. 

All discourse materials were imported into NVivo 15.0 for systematic coding. Deductively, four top-level analytical dimensions were constructed around action foundations, action purposes, action consequences, and institutional-cultural influences. Inductive coding was used to refine initial codes and subthemes within these predefined analytical dimensions. For example, initial codes such as "academic performance" and "personal traits" were identified through repeated engagement with the data and further compared during later stages of analysis. Table 2 provides illustrative examples of this coding process. Second-cycle coding was conducted to compare, merge, and reorganize the initial codes into more analytical subthemes. For instance, codes such as "academic performance" and "personal traits" were integrated into the subtheme of "individual competence". The coding system's saturation was carefully tested. As the number of analyzed texts increased, the emergence of new conceptual categories gradually declined. By the time the 14th text was coded, the coding outcomes had stabilized. Considering the potential volatility of saturation, an additional four interactive discourse samples were coded. The extracted conceptual elements showed a high degree of overlap with the existing coding scheme, and no new categories emerged. Potentially identifying personal details were removed, minimized, or replaced with generic descriptors where appropriate.

snippet.text: Recent interest in qualitative research methodology has created opportunities to explore conceptual relationships between qualitative and quantitative design and methods. Though it is accepted by some researchers that theory development may be achieved by qualitative case study research, these examples are rare. A qualitative case study, which blended notions of experimental method with qualitative research, has been described and the design rationale examined. By rendering more explicit the arguments and decision making processes that contribute to qualitative case study design, it is possible to gain a clearer assessment of a study's strengths and limitations, as well as contribute to our understanding of qualitative case study design and methodology.

documents.title: How primary health care teams perceive the integration of oral health care into their practice: A qualitative study
documents.snippet:
Following a thematic content analysis, four phases of qualitative analysis were identified as detailed by Bengtsson [23]: 1) decontextualization; 2) recontextualization; 3) categorization; and 4) compilation. Each of these stages was revised by other research team members who had deep knowledge on the integration concept in different disciplines. The involvement of an interdisciplinary research team prevented errors in data analysis, personal and interpretation bias, and ensured that no relevant data were excluded, thereby maintaining the confirmability and the credibility of the analysis [25]. 

In the phase of decontextualization, transcription of data was performed with repeated examination of recorded data by the first author (HH). Debriefing and reflexive field notes made it possible to better understand the context and the participants' discourse. Then, an "inductive open coding process" followed [26]. The content areas were identified and accordingly, the text was divided into meaning units, which were subsequently condensed and transformed into codes. The use of a code explanation document facilitated the tracking of coding decisions, and maximized the dependability of the data analysis. 

In the recontextualization phase, codes were reviewed against the original interview transcriptions. The research team regularly and thoroughly discussed uncertainties in coding and interpretation, and obtained agreement to ensure the study's credibility. 

In the phase of categorization, codes with similar conceptual content (meaning units) were grouped to identify the themes (Table 1). 

Finally, the last stage (compilation) comprised analysis and interpretation. Although descriptive, the manifest analysis was followed by a latent analysis to understand hidden meanings of the original texts. 

In the data interpretation, similarities and differences in rural and urban settings as well as the literature findings were considered, to maximize the transferability and authenticity of the research. Trustworthiness of the study was maximized by using principal guidelines in qualitative research [26]. A respondent validation was performed with 5 individuals. 

Data analysis was conducted manually and was assisted by the use of Atlas-ti software (ATLAS-ti Scientific Software Development GmbH, Berlin, Germany). Consolidated criteria for reporting qualitative research (COREQ) were followed.

documents.snippet: This qualitative research is driven by a social constructivist epistemology, recognizing the impact of contextual factors on interpersonal actions, viewing reality as dynamic and socially constructed, and interpreting human realities as shared and co-constructed meanings. Inductive qualitative thematic analysis was chosen to analyze the data because there is little literature on the research topic. 24,25 The following iterative coding methods were used: (1) familiarization of data, (2) generating initial codes, (3) combining codes into themes, (4) reviewing themes, (5) determining the significance of themes, and (6) reporting of findings. 24 The analysis began with reading the transcripts by two authors (S.V.S., S.V.) to gain a global understanding of the content of the data. The data were coded by S.V.S. and S.V. and the coding framework was discussed on various occasions (weekly meetings between S.V.S. and S.V., and project group meetings every 6 weeks) and validated by all other authors. 5][26] Both coders independently conducted a primary analysis of five transcripts (generating initial codes) and compared them with each other. S.V.S. then combined codes into themes. 5][26] SVS established relationships between the different codes to establish an overarching conceptual scheme with provisional themes and subthemes, which was discussed, reviewed, and validated by the authors (S.V., K.C., L.D., and S.D.). The final agreed-upon coding scheme was then applied to all transcripts. S.V.S. and S.V. independently used the conceptual coding scheme on the same interview transcripts to check for the validity and coherence of the codes and themes. The conceptual coding scheme was tested as such for multiple transcripts and adjusted where necessary by the project group until the researchers arrived at a coding scheme that represented each coder's insights and was considered valid by the project group. Finally, this coding scheme was applied to the transcripts in a final coding round. The coding scheme (including main themes and subthemes) and associated quotes were structured into a table and used to create our final analysis.

attempts.answer:
Overview: From Frames to Blends in Scientific Hypothesis Work
Conceptual blending integrates selected elements and relations from two or more mental spaces into a new space, producing emergent structure that yields creative, often surprising insights; this process underwrites metaphor, analogical reasoning, and understanding of novel concepts, and it operates as a routine mechanism in scientific and everyday reasoning <cite id="e3fa57bc-0">Conceptual Blending describes selective projection of elements and relational structures across mental spaces to form a blended space with emergent structure, enabling creativity, inference, and understanding of novel concepts</cite> <cite id="e3fa57bc-1">Blending creates new insights via partial matches between inputs, projecting selective features into a blended space that develops dynamic structures</cite> <cite id="e3fa57bc-2">Blending merges distinct domains into unified mental representations, exemplified by the planetary model of the atom, and is central to creative thinking and deep learning</cite> <cite id="e3fa57bc-4">CB is a set of cognitive operations for combining frames from different domains, producing new meaning and compressions that structure otherwise diffuse ranges of meaning</cite>. During hypothesis formation, researchers deploy “semantic frames” (stable conceptual structures and heuristics) to frame problems, map between domains, and iteratively reconfigure partial matches; the resulting conceptual blends then guide specific predictions and designs for testing <cite id="1f57f572-0">Conceptual metaphor maps concrete experiences onto abstract domains and is part of a continuum with blending and framing; blending integrates multiple domain networks with selected contrasts to produce novel conceptual constructions</cite> <cite id="1f57f572-3">Metaphors bridge old and new to enable cognitive shifts and serve heuristic, catachrestic, exegetical, theory-constitutive, and explanatory functions in science</cite>.

How Semantic Framing Catalyzes Blending
Semantic frames supply aligned concepts, relations, and constraints that make cross-domain combination tractable. A frame defines focal entities, causal schemas, and evaluation criteria; when two frames collide (double-scope), their partial compatibility sets up a blended space where only some inferences carry over, producing novelty at the interface. Frames also stabilize the core of what must be preserved (e.g., a research program’s hard core) while allowing auxiliary assumptions to be modified to resolve anomalies, which protects conceptual integrity while permitting creative accommodation and hypothesis revision <cite id="e3fa57bc-1">Selective projection of features from diverse scenarios into a single blended space generates new insights</cite> <cite id="e3fa57bc-2">Blending integrates distinct concepts such as planetary motion and atomic structure to create new models</cite> <cite id="1f57f572-4">Blending uses double-scope frames over clashing inputs, with composition, completion, and elaboration yielding emergent meaning and inferences</cite> <cite id="fc28e425-4">In Lakatosian programs, the negative heuristic fixes a hard core while the positive heuristic guides modification of auxiliary hypotheses to eliminate anomalies and generate new predictions</cite>.

Mechanisms that Generate Novelty and Testability
Blends arise from three coupled mechanisms: (1) partial matching and metonymic “bridging,” which preserve only shared roles/relations across frames; (2) compression of background knowledge and entailments, which produces emergent regularities and counter-inferences; and (3) boundary setting, which delimits where mappings hold. These mechanisms directly instantiate novelty: the planetary model’s gravitational orbits applied to electrons generated falsifiable predictions (e.g., spectral lines, quantization), and Lakatosian “auxiliary clauses” add testable predictions while protecting the program core from immediate refutation <cite id="1f57f572-2">CMT explains stable mappings, while CBT explains online integration via selective projection and vital relations compression, with dynamic blending networks extending metaphorical meaning</cite> <cite id="e3fa57bc-1">Blending integrates partial input features into a unique space whose structure develops dynamically, enabling new insights</cite> <cite id="1f57f572-3">Metaphorical bridging of new and old domains is the mechanism enabling cognitive shifts and heuristic functions in science</cite> <cite id="fc28e425-2">Scientists add auxiliary clauses to accommodate anomalies, expanding theory with at least equal content and making new predictions; progressive programs both solve past anomalies and anticipate new ones</cite> <cite id="fc28e425-3">The positive heuristic provides methods and modification pathways in the protective belt, maintaining the hard core while allowing refutation to occur at auxiliary levels</cite>.

A Process Model: From Framing to Hypothesis via Blending
1) Problem orientation and frame selection. Researchers adopt stable paradigms and program-level heuristics (negative/positive) that define acceptable core claims and method classes; these frames supply the “toolkit” of concepts and relations used to seek anomalies and mismatches <cite id="fc28e425-3">Research programs specify negative and positive heuristics: avoid core changes while pursuing modifications in auxiliary hypotheses and methods</cite> <cite id="1f57f572-1">Scientific texts progress from problematic situations (mismatches) to ideas, hypotheses, and deductions, with conventional metaphors and framing terms shaping hypothesis formation</cite>.
2) Domain mapping and blend construction. A source domain (e.g., mechanics) is mapped onto a target (e.g., atomic structure); only a partial match is constructed, and metonymic bridging ties roles (e.g., nucleus as “Sun,” electrons as “planetary orbiters”), compressing known laws to yield a novel model with emergent inferences (e.g., quantized orbits, spectral predictions) <cite id="e3fa57bc-0">Blending combines elements and relations from multiple spaces, producing emergent structures that enable creativity and understanding of novel concepts</cite> <cite id="e3fa57bc-2">The planetary model emerges from merging solar-system and atomic theory frames</cite> <cite id="1f57f572-4">Double-scope frames over clashing inputs drive composition, completion, and elaboration that generate new inferences</cite>.
3) Hypothesis articulation and test design. The blended space yields specific, often falsifiable predictions (e.g., energy levels and line spectra) and suggests methodologies (spectroscopy) consistent with the positive heuristic; auxiliary assumptions are formulated and linked to the program’s protective belt to absorb potential counterexamples while guarding the hard core <cite id="1f57f572-1">Hypotheses answer the formulated problem, combining logic and intuition; the hypothetic text organizes researcher terms into testable conjectures</cite> <cite id="fc28e425-2">Each new theory in a Lakatosian series adds auxiliary clauses to accommodate anomalies and makes new successful predictions</cite> <cite id="fc28e425-3">The positive heuristic guides where to modify auxiliary hypotheses, and empirical progress is tied to theoretical progress</cite>.
4) Evaluation and revision. Replication outcomes and anomalies trigger re-framing and re-blending: boundary conditions are adjusted, mappings are re-evaluated, and new metaphors supplant old ones as programs degenerate or progress; this iterative process yields fruitfulness when programs accumulate new predictions and withstand cumulative stress tests <cite id="fc28e425-2">Auxiliary clauses can add boundary conditions (e.g., context-dependent effects) to preserve programmatic coherence while addressing failures, with optimism that future corroborations may follow</cite> <cite id="fc28e425-3">Progressive programs solve past anomalies and generate new, supported predictions; degenerating programs accommodate anomalies without new support</cite> <cite id="1f57f572-3">Metaphors evolve in function and form as sciences develop; conceptual systems and explanatory functions are continually reshaped</cite>.

Why Frames Matter: Constraints, Guidance, and Fruitfulness
Frames do not eliminate selection—they define what counts as “relevant” mapping and which auxiliary assumptions are permissible. By anchoring a hard core and prescribing a positive heuristic, programs keep hypothesis spaces from drifting into incoherence; yet they remain generative because auxiliary belts can expand, introduce new relations, and suggest novel mechanisms and measurements. Empirically, students and scientists face the same challenge: without scaffolds, blending can produce vacuous or incoherent combinations; with guided frames (e.g., anchoring to evidence, method heuristics), blending reliably connects prior knowledge to novel insights and testable predictions <cite id="fc28e425-0">Blending scaffolds can help learners identify meaningful intersections among ideas and merge them with evidence to form integrated models, addressing difficulties in unguided blending</cite> <cite id="fc28e425-3">Negative heuristics constrain core changes (fruitfulness guardrails), while positive heuristics direct productive modifications and experimentation</cite> <cite id="1f57f572-1">Conventional scientific metaphors and structured subtexts (problem → idea → hypothesis → substantiation → deduction) channel metaphorical resources into progressive hypothesis development</cite>.

Evidence From Practice and Education
- Case-based learning and physics sensemaking: learners who blend domain frames (e.g., gravitation and electromagnetism) build integrated models that clarify conflicting phenomena and propose tests; guided blending around materials and evidence increases the novelty and coherence of their hypotheses <cite id="fc28e425-0">Blending supported student sensemaking in physics, creative engagement with complex phenomena via metaphors, and integration of math and physics concepts; scaffolds (multi-frame highlighting, anchoring evidence) structured discussions to discover novel relationships and integrated models</cite>.
- Scientific text analysis: hypothesis-rich texts systematically deploy conventional metaphors, dead metaphors, and original metaphors; these metaphorical layers construct domain mappings and blending networks that drive idea and hypothesis formation, with boundary-setting terms delimiting where analogies apply <cite id="1f57f572-1">Scientific texts progress through problematic situations to hypotheses and deductions; metaphor types (conventional, dead, original) build metaphorical models and trace domains used for new knowledge production</cite>.
- Domain cross-fertilization: new fields often “re-frame” old domains (e.g., economics borrowing biology and physiology), which introduces novel blends that seed hypotheses and terminologies; as evidence accumulates, metaphors are adjusted or replaced, refining program-level frames <cite id="1f57f572-3">Metaphorical bridging is central to forming scientific ideas; conceptual metaphors link disciplines (e.g., economy-as-organism) and shape thinking, evolving with breakthroughs and shifts</cite>.

Practical Implications for Research Practice
- Frame auditing: periodically review program-level frames (core assumptions, positive/negative heuristics) to ensure they remain enabling of empirical progress; allow boundary-condition hypotheses to absorb failures rather than triggering premature program rejection <cite id="fc28e425-2">Progressive programs add auxiliary clauses and make new successful predictions; degenerating programs only accommodate anomalies without support</cite> <cite id="fc28e425-3">The protective belt is modified per the positive heuristic; empirical and theoretical progress are linked</cite>.
- Cross-domain ideation: deliberately import mappings from structurally similar domains (e.g., network flow for information spread), then “cut” the metaphor at its conceptual joints—only reassert partial relations—to form a testable hypothesis blend <cite id="e3fa57bc-0">Emergent structures in blending account for phenomena ranging from everyday metaphor to scientific invention</cite> <cite id="1f57f572-0">Conceptual metaphors and blending integrate multiple mappings into networks, enabling creative combinations</cite>.
- Evidence-anchored completion: use available data and theory snippets as “anchoring evidence” to constrain the blended space, so completion and elaboration steps yield falsifiable predictions and suggest concrete measurement strategies <cite id="fc28e425-0">Anchoring evidence guides merging of ideas with peers’ content, structuring input spaces to discover novel relationships and transform them into integrated models</cite> <cite id="1f57f572-4">Blending’s completion integrates selected background with fused ideas to generate inferences and reasoning that can be tested</cite>.
- Boundary-condition hypothesis testing: when anomalies appear, propose boundary-condition clauses rather than immediately reinterpreting the core; this preserves conceptual integrity and focuses creative effort on protective-belt revisions and new predictions <cite id="fc28e425-2">Scientists may add boundary conditions (e.g., context-dependent effects) to maintain program coherence and accommodate failures while anticipating corroboration</cite>.

Boundaries and Pitfalls
Blending can generate empty verbiage unless frames tightly constrain role preservation and testability. Overprotective negative heuristics can suppress progress; degenerative programs stagnate when only boundary tweaks are applied without expanding predictive content. The latter is built on the productive model of scientific cognition and communication which comprises a problematic situation, problem, idea, hypothesis, substantiation and deduction (Kozhina, 2002), causing sense production in the text. The problematic situation arises when the researcher identifies mismatched facts of existing knowledge, the problem deals with formulating the cognitive question, the idea presupposes search for a possible intuitive answer, the hypothesis contains an answer based both on logic and intuition, substantiation is a detailed logic answer and deduction is a final researcher's answer. These parts of the model determine the specificity of scientific subtexts as components of the scientific text constructed to develop the conception. 

The problematic situation and problem are presented in the problem formulating subtext, the idea and hypothesis -in the hypothetic subtext, substantiation -in the substantiating text and deduction -in the deducing subtext. The problem formulating text represents a gap in existing knowledge that causes a research question. This subtext has numerous terms from theories, among which there are conventional scientific metaphors. The hypothetic text gives an answer to the problematic question in the form of the researcher's terms and their definitions logically organized. The substantiating text is characterized by the researcher's metaphorical terms in complex sentences with long logical chains. In the deducing text the researcher outlines the chosen concept and gives the final answer to the problematic question using lexical units denoting righteousness. 

Our study of metaphors in various scientific texts revealed that researchers usually use three types of metaphors: conventional scientific metaphors denoting existing knowledge shared by a scientific community, dead metaphors, mapping the mental world and noticed by linguists, and a researcher's original metaphors which create and convey new knowledge. Snippet: Although both Conceptual Metaphor Theory (CMT) and Conceptual Blending Theory (CBT) have made significant contributions to metaphor research, each exhibits limitations when applied independently to literary discourse analysis. CMT primarily accounts for stable crossdomain correspondences between source and target domains, thereby revealing the conceptual foundations of metaphorical cognition. However, it is relatively limited in explaining contextual emergence, semantic creativity, and the dynamic extension of highly innovative literary metaphors. In contrast, CBT emphasizes online meaning construction through the interaction of multiple mental spaces, selective projection, and vital relations compression. Nevertheless, when applied in isolation, it may underemphasize the relatively stable conceptual structures that support metaphor comprehension. To address these limitations, this study integrates CMT and CBT within a unified analytical framework. Within this framework, CMT accounts for the relatively stable conceptual mappings underlying metaphorical structures, while CBT explains the dynamic construction of meaning in specific narrative contexts. The analytical focus therefore shifts from static conceptual mapping to dynamic conceptual integration. More specifically, the analytical procedure consists of three interrelated stages. First, Conceptual Metaphor Theory (CMT) is employed to identify source-target mappings and underlying conceptual correspondences in metaphorical expressions. Second, Conceptual Blending Theory (CBT) is applied to examine interactions among multiple mental spaces, including selective projection, role integration, and structural compression. Finally, the study explores how metaphorical meaning is progressively extended within narrative contexts, thereby forming what is termed a "dynamic blending network." The term "dynamic blending network" refers to a hierarchical and evolving conceptual integration structure in which metaphorical meaning is continuously reconstructed through recursive interactions among mental spaces, contextual reinforcement, and semantic compression. Rather than emerging instantaneously, metaphorical meaning develops progressively through narrative unfolding, enabling the accumulation of additional thematic, psychological, and satirical layers in Fortress Besieged. In this model (see Figure 1), the metaphor "the besieged fortress" functions as a recursive cognitive node rather than a fixed symbolic structure. Semantic frames supply aligned concepts, relations, and constraints that make cross-domain combination tractable. A frame defines focal entities, causal schemas, and evaluation criteria; when two frames collide (double-scope), their partial compatibility sets up a blended space where only some inferences carry over, producing novelty at the interface. Frames also stabilize the core of what must be preserved (e.g., a research program’s hard core) while allowing auxiliary assumptions to be modified to resolve anomalies, which protects conceptual integrity while permitting creative accommodation and hypothesis revision <cite id="e3fa57bc-1">Selective projection of features from diverse scenarios into a single blended space generates new insights</cite> <cite id="e3fa57bc-2">Blending integrates distinct concepts such as planetary motion and atomic structure to create new models</cite> <cite id="1f57f572-4">Blending uses double-scope frames over clashing inputs, with composition, completion, and elaboration yielding emergent meaning and inferences</cite> <cite id="fc28e425-4">In Lakatosian programs, the negative heuristic fixes a hard core while the positive heuristic guides modification of auxiliary hypotheses to eliminate anomalies and generate new predictions</cite>.

Mechanisms that Generate Novelty and Testability
Blends arise from three coupled mechanisms: (1) partial matching and metonymic “bridging,” which preserve only shared roles/relations across frames; (2) compression of background knowledge and entailments, which produces emergent regularities and counter-inferences; and (3) boundary setting, which delimits where mappings hold. These mechanisms directly instantiate novelty: the planetary model’s gravitational orbits applied to electrons generated falsifiable predictions (e.g., spectral lines, quantization), and Lakatosian “auxiliary clauses” add testable predictions while protecting the program core from immediate refutation <cite id="1f57f572-2">CMT explains stable mappings, while CBT explains online integration via selective projection and vital relations compression, with dynamic blending networks extending metaphorical meaning</cite> <cite id="e3fa57bc-1">Blending integrates partial input features into a unique space whose structure develops dynamically, enabling new insights</cite> <cite id="1f57f572-3">Metaphorical bridging of new and old domains is the mechanism enabling cognitive shifts and heuristic functions in science</cite> <cite id="fc28e425-2">Scientists add auxiliary clauses to accommodate anomalies, expanding theory with at least equal content and making new predictions; progressive programs both solve past anomalies and anticipate new ones</cite> <cite id="fc28e425-3">The positive heuristic provides methods and modification pathways in the protective belt, maintaining the hard core while allowing refutation to occur at auxiliary levels</cite>.

A Process Model: From Framing to Hypothesis via Blending
1) Problem orientation and frame selection. Researchers adopt stable paradigms and program-level heuristics (negative/positive) that define acceptable core claims and method classes; these frames supply the “toolkit” of concepts and relations used to seek anomalies and mismatches <cite id="fc28e425-3">Research programs specify negative and positive heuristics: avoid core changes while pursuing modifications in auxiliary hypotheses and methods</cite> <cite id="1f57f572-1">Scientific texts progress from problematic situations (mismatches) to ideas, hypotheses, and deductions, with conventional metaphors and framing terms shaping hypothesis formation</cite>.
2) Domain mapping and blend construction. A source domain (e.g., mechanics) is mapped onto a target (e.g., atomic structure); only a partial match is constructed, and metonymic bridging ties roles (e.g., nucleus as “Sun,” electrons as “planetary orbiters”), compressing known laws to yield a novel model with emergent inferences (e.g., quantized orbits, spectral predictions) <cite id="e3fa57bc-0">Blending combines elements and relations from multiple spaces, producing emergent structures that enable creativity and understanding of novel concepts</cite> <cite id="e3fa57bc-2">The planetary model emerges from merging solar-system and atomic theory frames</cite> <cite id="1f57f572-4">Double-scope frames over clashing inputs drive composition, completion, and elaboration that generate new inferences</cite>.
3) Hypothesis articulation and test design. The blended space yields specific, often falsifiable predictions (e.g., energy levels and line spectra) and suggests methodologies (spectroscopy) consistent with the positive heuristic; auxiliary assumptions are formulated and linked to the program’s protective belt to absorb potential counterexamples while guarding the hard core <cite id="1f57f572-1">Hypotheses answer the formulated problem, combining logic and intuition; the hypothetic text organizes researcher terms into testable conjectures</cite> <cite id="fc28e425-2">Each new theory in a Lakatosian series adds auxiliary clauses to accommodate anomalies and makes new successful predictions</cite> <cite id="fc28e425-3">The positive heuristic guides where to modify auxiliary hypotheses, and empirical progress is tied to theoretical progress</cite>.
4) Evaluation and revision. Replication outcomes and anomalies trigger re-framing and re-blending: boundary conditions are adjusted, mappings are re-evaluated, and new metaphors supplant old ones as programs degenerate or progress; this iterative process yields fruitfulness when programs accumulate new predictions and withstand cumulative stress tests <cite id="fc28e425-2">Auxiliary clauses can add boundary conditions (e.g., context-dependent effects) to preserve programmatic coherence while addressing failures, with optimism that future corroborations may follow</cite> <cite id="fc28e425-3">Progressive programs solve past anomalies and generate new, supported predictions; degenerating programs accommodate anomalies without new support</cite> <cite id="1f57f572-3">Metaphors evolve in function and form as sciences develop; conceptual systems and explanatory functions are continually reshaped</cite>.

Why Frames Matter: Constraints, Guidance, and Fruitfulness
Frames do not eliminate selection—they define what counts as “relevant” mapping and which auxiliary assumptions are permissible. By anchoring a hard core and prescribing a positive heuristic, programs keep hypothesis spaces from drifting into incoherence; yet they remain generative because auxiliary belts can expand, introduce new relations, and suggest novel mechanisms and measurements. Empirically, students and scientists face the same challenge: without scaffolds, blending can produce vacuous or incoherent combinations; with guided frames (e.g., anchoring to evidence, method heuristics), blending reliably connects prior knowledge to novel insights and testable predictions <cite id="fc28e425-0">Blending scaffolds can help learners identify meaningful intersections among ideas and merge them with evidence to form integrated models, addressing difficulties in unguided blending</cite> <cite id="fc28e425-3">Negative heuristics constrain core changes (fruitfulness guardrails), while positive heuristics direct productive modifications and experimentation</cite> <cite id="1f57f572-1">Conventional scientific metaphors and structured subtexts (problem → idea → hypothesis → substantiation → deduction) channel metaphorical resources into progressive hypothesis development</cite>.

Evidence From Practice and Education
- Case-based learning and physics sensemaking: learners who blend domain frames (e.g., gravitation and electromagnetism) build integrated models that clarify conflicting phenomena and propose tests; guided blending around materials and evidence increases the novelty and coherence of their hypotheses <cite id="fc28e425-0">Blending supported student sensemaking in physics, creative engagement with complex phenomena via metaphors, and integration of math and physics concepts; scaffolds (multi-frame highlighting, anchoring evidence) structured discussions to discover novel relationships and integrated models</cite>.
- Scientific text analysis: hypothesis-rich texts systematically deploy conventional metaphors, dead metaphors, and original metaphors; these metaphorical layers construct domain mappings and blending networks that drive idea and hypothesis formation, with boundary-setting terms delimiting where analogies apply <cite id="1f57f572-1">Scientific texts progress through problematic situations to hypotheses and deductions; metaphor types (conventional, dead, original) build metaphorical models and trace domains used for new knowledge production</cite>.
- Domain cross-fertilization: new fields often “re-frame” old domains (e.g., economics borrowing biology and physiology), which introduces novel blends that seed hypotheses and terminologies; as evidence accumulates, metaphors are adjusted or replaced, refining program-level frames <cite id="1f57f572-3">Metaphorical bridging is central to forming scientific ideas; conceptual metaphors link disciplines (e.g., economy-as-organism) and shape thinking, evolving with breakthroughs and shifts</cite>.

Practical Implications for Research Practice
- Frame auditing: periodically review program-level frames (core assumptions, positive/negative heuristics) to ensure they remain enabling of empirical progress; allow boundary-condition hypotheses to absorb failures rather than triggering premature program rejection <cite id="fc28e425-2">Progressive programs add auxiliary clauses and make new successful predictions; degenerating programs only accommodate anomalies without support</cite> <cite id="fc28e425-3">The protective belt is modified per the positive heuristic; empirical and theoretical progress are linked</cite>.
- Cross-domain ideation: deliberately import mappings from structurally similar domains (e.g., network flow for information spread), then “cut” the metaphor at its conceptual joints—only reassert partial relations—to form a testable hypothesis blend <cite id="e3fa57bc-0">Emergent structures in blending account for phenomena ranging from everyday metaphor to scientific invention</cite> <cite id="1f57f572-0">Conceptual metaphors and blending integrate multiple mappings into networks, enabling creative combinations</cite>.
- Evidence-anchored completion: use available data and theory snippets as “anchoring evidence” to constrain the blended space, so completion and elaboration steps yield falsifiable predictions and suggest concrete measurement strategies <cite id="fc28e425-0">Anchoring evidence guides merging of ideas with peers’ content, structuring input spaces to discover novel relationships and transform them into integrated models</cite> <cite id="1f57f572-4">Blending’s completion integrates selected background with fused ideas to generate inferences and reasoning that can be tested</cite>.
- Boundary-condition hypothesis testing: when anomalies appear, propose boundary-condition clauses rather than immediately reinterpreting the core; this preserves conceptual integrity and focuses creative effort on protective-belt revisions and new predictions <cite id="fc28e425-2">Scientists may add boundary conditions (e.g., context-dependent effects) to maintain program coherence and accommodate failures while anticipating corroboration</cite>.

Boundaries and Pitfalls
Blending can generate empty verbiage unless frames tightly constrain role preservation and testability. Overprotective negative heuristics can suppress progress; degenerative programs stagnate when only boundary tweaks are applied without expanding predictive content. Effective hypothesis formation requires iterative re-framing: adjust mapping assumptions, revise protective belts, and prune non-predictive entailments to maintain empirical leverage <cite id="fc28e425-3">Progress requires conserving the core while adding techniques and modifying auxiliary ideas; refutation occurs at the belt, preserving core stability</cite> <cite id="fc28e425-2">Progressive programs both solve prior anomalies and produce new, supported predictions; degenerating programs fail this test</cite> <cite id="1f57f572-2">Stable mappings (CMT) plus dynamic integration (CBT) prevent under- or over-specification; integrating both addresses limits of metaphor-only or blend-only accounts</cite>.

Takeaway
Semantic framing provides the scaffolding for conceptual blending during hypothesis formation: it supplies the domains, relations, and heuristics to construct partial, cross-domain matches; the emergent structures of blending yield novel inferences and testable predictions; and program-level constraints protect fruitfulness while enabling progressive theory modification. Together, frames make blend novelty actionable—turning metaphor and analogy into concrete hypotheses that can be scrutinized, refined, or replaced as evidence accumulates <cite id="e3fa57bc-0">Blending’s emergent structures enable creativity and understanding of novel concepts by combining existing spaces</cite> <cite id="e3fa57bc-1">Partial matching and projection into a new blended space create new insights and structures</cite> <cite id="1f57f572-0">Framing and blending integrate multiple domain mappings into networks that produce creative combinations</cite> <cite id="fc28e425-2">Hypothesis series grow by adding auxiliary clauses that accommodate anomalies and generate new predictions, defining progress</cite> <cite id="fc28e425-3">Program-level heuristics and protective belts channel modification to maintain core commitments while enabling innovation</cite> <cite id="fc28e425-0">Scaffolded blending helps learners discover novel relationships and integrate ideas into testable models</cite>.</answer>

Title: GLITTER: An AI-assisted Platform for Material-Grounded Asynchronous Discussion in Flipped Learning
Snippet: Conceptual blending describes how people naturally combine ideas from different domains to create new understanding. For example, when students learn about atomic structure, they might blend their knowledge of the solar system (planets orbiting the sun) with atomic theory (electrons around a nucleus) to form the "planetary model" of the atom. This cognitive process of merging distinct concepts into unified mental representations lies at the heart of creative thinking and deep learning [25]. In educational contexts, conceptual blending could become particularly valuable for asynchronous discussions because it helps students move beyond simply sharing isolated thoughts to actively synthesizing diverse perspectives into richer understanding. When students encounter multiple viewpoints in discussion forums, blending theory provides a framework for identifying meaningful connections and creating integrated insights that wouldn't emerge from individual posts alone. Conceptual Blending Theory offers a cognitive framework explaining how people integrate elements from different mental spaces to produce new ideas and understandings. Fauconnier and Turner argue that human learning and thinking fundamentally depend on such blending processes [27], which operate as routine, often subconscious mechanisms in everyday cognition, seamlessly combining disparate knowledge frames into unified mental representations [25]. This process represents a form of combinational creativity [7] that enables constructing metaphors, innovation through analogical reasoning, and abstract problem solving [54]. 

Prior research has demonstrated the benefits of computational tools that support conceptual blending for creative design [23]. Vis-iBlends [17] and VisiFit [16] proposed novel pipelines for blending visual objects to convey integrated meaning, while PopBlends automatically suggests conceptual blends of reference images [55]. Domain-specific applications include ICONATE [61] for icon generation through mixing different visual elements, FashionQ [35] for fashion design, and Artinter [18] for recombining style elements to facilitate communication. In a related approach, 3DALL-E [42] offers an ideation system that identifies granular conceptual elements and integrates them to create comprehensive prompts for text-to-image models. Conceptual blending has also informed design methodologies [33], underscoring its value as a framework for interactive tools that augment human reasoning and creativity. In educational contexts, conceptual blending theory explains how learners generate novel insights by merging multiple ideas or analogies.

Title: GLITTER: An AI-assisted Platform for Material-Grounded Asynchronous Discussion in Flipped Learning
Snippet: In educational contexts, conceptual blending theory explains how learners generate novel insights by merging multiple ideas or analogies. For example, blending has supported student sensemaking in physics by enabling integrated conceptual structures [45], helped students creatively engage with complex scientific phenomena through intuitive metaphors [30], and facilitated students' integration of mathematics and physics concepts during problemsolving [20,32]. Additionally, blending has been observed in collaborative small-group learning, where students jointly construct integrated mental models through social interaction, deepening their conceptual understanding of challenging topics such as quantum mechanics [31]. Conceptual blending can enrich material-based discussions by offering a structured framework for integrating diverse perspectives with learning materials, helping learners connect their ideas with peers' contributions to foster innovative thinking. By structuring discussions around specific materials, blending can drive students to creatively synthesize diverse ideas grounded in evidence. However, using conceptual blending in this context also poses challenges. Students often struggle to identify meaningful conceptual intersections between their ideas without guidance. Effective scaffolding is therefore essential to help students discover these conceptual connections, providing enough structure to focus their reasoning while still encouraging creative exploration of potential conceptual blends.

In educational contexts, conceptual blending theory explains how learners generate novel insights by merging multiple ideas or analogies. For example, blending has supported student sensemaking in physics by enabling integrated conceptual structures [45], helped students creatively engage with complex scientific phenomena through intuitive metaphors [30], and facilitated students' integration of mathematics and physics concepts during problemsolving [20,32]. Title: Evaluating the Development of Linguistic Metaphor Annotation in Mexican Spanish Popular Science Tweets
Snippet: According to conceptual metaphor theory (CMT), the fundamental feature of metaphor, as a cognitive phenomenon, lies in the conceptual mapping between source and target domains, i.e. a process whereby our understanding of concrete experiences is projected onto more abstract domains, facilitating comprehension and communication of complex ideas (Lakoff and Johnson, 1980).With this theoretical background in mind, it is vital to understand that linguistic metaphors are the linguistic expressions that manifest conceptual metaphors.In that regard, linguistic metaphors are made of language units, and they permeate various aspects of communication, from everyday conversation to specialized fields such as scientific communication, where they play a crucial role in shaping the way scientific concepts are articulated and understood by the public.

Furthermore, subsequent approaches within cognitive linguistics, such as conceptual blending challenged the notion of mapping as the sole foundation of the cognitive operation underlying metaphor.Instead, authors like Fauconnier and Turner (2008) hypothesize that metaphors are part of a continuum of mental operations (including metonymy and framing) where different domains are integrated into several networks within a mental space.In this integrated networks, specific features are selected for contrast, resulting in conceptual blending.Thus, conceptual metaphors are mental constructions resulting from the integration of multiple spaces and multiple mappings.

Title: Metaphors in “The Elements of Language” by E.Sapir
Snippet: In science metaphors are determined by many factors among which is a complex interaction of personal knowledge as a result of a person's activity in all spheres of life and scientific knowledge obtained from a particular field of knowledge. Both types of knowledge are structured in accordance with the dominant paradigm and presented in the form of a scientific text. The latter is built on the productive model of scientific cognition and communication which comprises a problematic situation, problem, idea, hypothesis, substantiation and deduction (Kozhina, 2002), causing sense production in the text. The problematic situation arises when the researcher identifies mismatched facts of existing knowledge, the problem deals with formulating the cognitive question, the idea presupposes search for a possible intuitive answer, the hypothesis contains an answer based both on logic and intuition, substantiation is a detailed logic answer and deduction is a final researcher's answer. These parts of the model determine the specificity of scientific subtexts as components of the scientific text constructed to develop the conception. 

The problematic situation and problem are presented in the problem formulating subtext, the idea and hypothesis -in the hypothetic subtext, substantiation -in the substantiating text and deduction -in the deducing subtext. The problem formulating text represents a gap in existing knowledge that causes a research question. This subtext has numerous terms from theories, among which there are conventional scientific metaphors. The hypothetic text gives an answer to the problematic question in the form of the researcher's terms and their definitions logically organized. The substantiating text is characterized by the researcher's metaphorical terms in complex sentences with long logical chains. In the deducing text the researcher outlines the chosen concept and gives the final answer to the problematic question using lexical units denoting righteousness. 

Our study of metaphors in various scientific texts revealed that researchers usually use three types of metaphors: conventional scientific metaphors denoting existing knowledge shared by a scientific community, dead metaphors, mapping the mental world and noticed by linguists, and a researcher's original metaphors which create and convey new knowledge. The analysis of these three types of metaphors allows constructing metaphorical models and tracing the domains which are used for new knowledge production.

Title: A Cognitive Study on the Meaning Construction Process of Novel Metaphors in Fortress Besieged from the Perspective of Conceptual Integration Theory
Snippet: Although both Conceptual Metaphor Theory (CMT) and Conceptual Blending Theory (CBT) have made significant contributions to metaphor research, each exhibits limitations when applied independently to literary discourse analysis. CMT primarily accounts for stable crossdomain correspondences between source and target domains, thereby revealing the conceptual foundations of metaphorical cognition. However, it is relatively limited in explaining contextual emergence, semantic creativity, and the dynamic extension of highly innovative literary metaphors. In contrast, CBT emphasizes online meaning construction through the interaction of multiple mental spaces, selective projection, and vital relations compression. Nevertheless, when applied in isolation, it may underemphasize the relatively stable conceptual structures that support metaphor comprehension. To address these limitations, this study integrates CMT and CBT within a unified analytical framework. Within this framework, CMT accounts for the relatively stable conceptual mappings underlying metaphorical structures, while CBT explains the dynamic construction of meaning in specific narrative contexts. The analytical focus therefore shifts from static conceptual mapping to dynamic conceptual integration. More specifically, the analytical procedure consists of three interrelated stages. First, Conceptual Metaphor Theory (CMT) is employed to identify source-target mappings and underlying conceptual correspondences in metaphorical expressions. Second, Conceptual Blending Theory (CBT) is applied to examine interactions among multiple mental spaces, including selective projection, role integration, and structural compression. Finally, the study explores how metaphorical meaning is progressively extended within narrative contexts, thereby forming what is termed a "dynamic blending network." The term "dynamic blending network" refers to a hierarchical and evolving conceptual integration structure in which metaphorical meaning is continuously reconstructed through recursive interactions among mental spaces, contextual reinforcement, and semantic compression. Rather than emerging instantaneously, metaphorical meaning develops progressively through narrative unfolding, enabling the accumulation of additional thematic, psychological, and satirical layers in Fortress Besieged. In this model (see Figure 1), the metaphor "the besieged fortress" functions as a recursive cognitive node rather than a fixed symbolic structure. Different narrative contexts repeatedly activate and reconfigure this blending network, allowing the metaphor to evolve from a representation of marital confinement into a broader conceptualization of human entrapment and existential survival.

Title: The Birth of Modern Economics and “Crossfertilization” of Sciences
Snippet: The legitimacy of metaphors as full-fledged members of scientific discourse has been causing continual debates. However, decades of research have proved the centrality of metaphors in the formation of scientific ideas and worldviews. "Metaphorical bridging of the new and old is precisely the mechanism that makes cognitive shifts possible. And for that reason metaphors function as far-reaching instruments for the theoretical language in science and scientific reasoning itself " (Radman 1997, p. 61). In science, metaphors perform at least five important functions: 1) a heuristic function that helps to visualize a new phenomenon; 2) a catachrestic function filling lexical gaps in terminology; 3) an exegetical function of transmitting concepts down to new generations of scientists (Mouton 2012); 4) a theory-constitutive function that ensures the creation of a conceptual system of a science (Boyd 1993); and finally, 5) an explanatory function which provides for the dissemination of knowledge (Resche 2012). 

Since its very birth, economics has been drawing heavily on the established sciences for their techniques, ideas, style, and terminology. The links of economics with other disciplines can be clearly discerned in conceptual metaphors. For example, when economists speak about 'economic growth' they equate the economy to some biological organism, thus establishing a link between economics and biology; or when journalists write that small business is 'the lifeblood of the economy' the connection between economics and physiology is easily recognized. Such interaction of sciences is called 'crossfertilization'. By the standard definition, conceptual metaphors are systematic sets of 'mappings' or correspondences across conceptual domains (Lakoff and Johnson 1980, p. 7). Interpreted as a systematic phenomenon, these correspondences form metaphoric paradigms which shape scientific thinking over more or less lengthy periods of time, or sometimes entire epochs, but also are subject to modifications or even replacement due to scientific breakthroughs, shifts in technology, changes in social and cultural life, but mainly due to changes in the worldview.

snippet.text:
In science metaphors are determined by many factors among which is a complex interaction of personal knowledge as a result of a person's activity in all spheres of life and scientific knowledge obtained from a particular field of knowledge. Both types of knowledge are structured in accordance with the dominant paradigm and presented in the form of a scientific text. The latter is built on the productive model of scientific cognition and communication which comprises a problematic situation, problem, idea, hypothesis, substantiation and deduction (Kozhina, 2002), causing sense production in the text. The problematic situation arises when the researcher identifies mismatched facts of existing knowledge, the problem deals with formulating the cognitive question, the idea presupposes search for a possible intuitive answer, the hypothesis contains an answer based both on logic and intuition, substantiation is a detailed logic answer and deduction is a final researcher's answer. These parts of the model determine the specificity of scientific subtexts as components of the scientific text constructed to develop the conception. 

The problematic situation and problem are presented in the problem formulating subtext, the idea and hypothesis -in the hypothetic subtext, substantiation -in the substantiating text and deduction -in the deducing subtext. The problem formulating text represents a gap in existing knowledge that causes a research question. This subtext has numerous terms from theories, among which there are conventional scientific metaphors. The hypothetic text gives an answer to the problematic question in the form of the researcher's terms and their definitions logically organized. The substantiating text is characterized by the researcher's metaphorical terms in complex sentences with long logical chains. In the deducing text the researcher outlines the chosen concept and gives the final answer to the problematic question using lexical units denoting righteousness. 

Our study of metaphors in various scientific texts revealed that researchers usually use three types of metaphors: conventional scientific metaphors denoting existing knowledge shared by a scientific community, dead metaphors, mapping the mental world and noticed by linguists, and a researcher's original metaphors which create and convey new knowledge. The analysis of these three types of metaphors allows constructing metaphorical models and tracing the domains which are used for new knowledge production.

snippet.text: Although both Conceptual Metaphor Theory (CMT) and Conceptual Blending Theory (CBT) have made significant contributions to metaphor research, each exhibits limitations when applied independently to literary discourse analysis. CMT primarily accounts for stable crossdomain correspondences between source and target domains, thereby revealing the conceptual foundations of metaphorical cognition. However, it is relatively limited in explaining contextual emergence, semantic creativity, and the dynamic extension of highly innovative literary metaphors. In contrast, CBT emphasizes online meaning construction through the interaction of multiple mental spaces, selective projection, and vital relations compression. Nevertheless, when applied in isolation, it may underemphasize the relatively stable conceptual structures that support metaphor comprehension. To address these limitations, this study integrates CMT and CBT within a unified analytical framework. Within this framework, CMT accounts for the relatively stable conceptual mappings underlying metaphorical structures, while CBT explains the dynamic construction of meaning in specific narrative contexts. The analytical focus therefore shifts from static conceptual mapping to dynamic conceptual integration. More specifically, the analytical procedure consists of three interrelated stages. First, Conceptual Metaphor Theory (CMT) is employed to identify source-target mappings and underlying conceptual correspondences in metaphorical expressions. Second, Conceptual Blending Theory (CBT) is applied to examine interactions among multiple mental spaces, including selective projection, role integration, and structural compression. Finally, the study explores how metaphorical meaning is progressively extended within narrative contexts, thereby forming what is termed a "dynamic blending network." The term "dynamic blending network" refers to a hierarchical and evolving conceptual integration structure in which metaphorical meaning is continuously reconstructed through recursive interactions among mental spaces, contextual reinforcement, and semantic compression. Rather than emerging instantaneously, metaphorical meaning develops progressively through narrative unfolding, enabling the accumulation of additional thematic, psychological, and satirical layers in Fortress Besieged. In this model (see Figure 1), the metaphor "the besieged fortress" functions as a recursive cognitive node rather than a fixed symbolic structure. Different narrative contexts repeatedly activate and reconfigure this blending network, allowing the metaphor to evolve from a representation of marital confinement into a broader conceptualization of human entrapment and existential survival.

snippet.text:
The legitimacy of metaphors as full-fledged members of scientific discourse has been causing continual debates. However, decades of research have proved the centrality of metaphors in the formation of scientific ideas and worldviews. "Metaphorical bridging of the new and old is precisely the mechanism that makes cognitive shifts possible. And for that reason metaphors function as far-reaching instruments for the theoretical language in science and scientific reasoning itself " (Radman 1997, p. 61). In science, metaphors perform at least five important functions: 1) a heuristic function that helps to visualize a new phenomenon; 2) a catachrestic function filling lexical gaps in terminology; 3) an exegetical function of transmitting concepts down to new generations of scientists (Mouton 2012); 4) a theory-constitutive function that ensures the creation of a conceptual system of a science (Boyd 1993); and finally, 5) an explanatory function which provides for the dissemination of knowledge (Resche 2012). 

Since its very birth, economics has been drawing heavily on the established sciences for their techniques, ideas, style, and terminology. The links of economics with other disciplines can be clearly discerned in conceptual metaphors. For example, when economists speak about 'economic growth' they equate the economy to some biological organism, thus establishing a link between economics and biology; or when journalists write that small business is 'the lifeblood of the economy' the connection between economics and physiology is easily recognized. Such interaction of sciences is called 'crossfertilization'. By the standard definition, conceptual metaphors are systematic sets of 'mappings' or correspondences across conceptual domains (Lakoff and Johnson 1980, p. 7). Interpreted as a systematic phenomenon, these correspondences form metaphoric paradigms which shape scientific thinking over more or less lengthy periods of time, or sometimes entire epochs, but also are subject to modifications or even replacement due to scientific breakthroughs, shifts in technology, changes in social and cultural life, but mainly due to changes in the worldview.
