Overview: Framing and blending as cognitive-epistemic engines of theory change
- Semantic framing shapes what is seen and how it is structured: it foregrounds certain features of a phenomenon, aligns concepts via analogy, and defines the community’s problem space and criteria of adequacy. Conceptual blending then drives theory change by integrating source/target domains or paradigms into a new blended space, producing novel predictions, models, and reorganizations of explanatory concepts. Together, framing selects and bounds the inputs; blending synthesizes them into richer or alternative theories. <cite id="b50dab97-0">Frames have been used to analyze scientific concepts and conceptual change with respect to Kuhn’s approach of scientific revolutions, enabling distinctions between inter-/intra-conceptual change, structural vs content change, and conceptual enrichment as opposed to change</cite> <cite id="fa7920dc-1">Conceptual integration theory posits that elements from two or more conceptual packages merge into a qualitatively new higher-level package (the blend) formed by shared structure (generic space) and emergent content</cite> <cite id="ada0e252-0">Cognitive blending integrates two input mental spaces via mapping across frames and cognitive models, yielding blended spaces where new meaning and insight emerge</cite>.

How semantic framing shapes the research process and theory change
- Problem selection and representation. <cite id="b50dab97-2">Framings (often metaphor-based) are crucial for theory building and hypothesizing in science; in Alzheimer’s disease, framings such as “cascade” shape the understanding of the disease and steer attention and evaluative norms, showing that the same phenomenon can be “understood” differently depending on how it is framed</cite>. <cite id="b50dab97-3">Across social sciences, “frame” and “framing” have become central for building relational sciences, with Popper arguing that frameworks need not be incommensurable in the strong sense that blocks rational communication, supporting the idea that shifts in frames can be critically discussed toward objective truth</cite>. <cite id="b50dab97-4">Frames provide stereotyped, visualized, and generalized structures that fix analogies and generalizations, and have been used to represent and analyze scientific concepts and conceptual change in philosophy of science</cite>.
- Integration and accommodation of anomalies. <cite id="b50dab97-0">Analyses of conceptual change distinguish assimilation (adding concepts without altering structure), accommodation (conflict leading to replacement/modification), and enrichment (adding content without changing structure), clarifying how reframing mediates whether anomalies prompt puzzle-solving or paradigm adjustment</cite> <cite id="fa7920dc-3">Conceptual change theory explains that new concepts may be assimilated or accommodated, with accommodation producing replacement or modification of existing structures</cite>.
- Evaluation and acceptability. <cite id="ada0e252-2">Alternative views of scientific revolutions (e.g., Cohen’s staged model) emphasize that change begins with individual conceptual advances and culminates in acceptance, with judgments depending on impact on textbooks and expert evaluation, linking reframing/blending products to social-cognitive criteria of theory acceptance</cite>.
- Interdisciplinarity and method. <cite id="b50dab97-0">Graph-theoretic formalization and ontology-building for frames show how structured representations can track conceptual relations and support systematic comparison over time, facilitating evidence-based reconstructions of theory change</cite>.

How conceptual blending shapes the research process and theory change
- Generative synthesis across domains. <cite id="fa7920dc-0">Conceptual blending enables learners and researchers to merge multiple ideas or analogies, creating integrated conceptual structures that support sensemaking in physics and cross-domain integration (e.g., math/physics, quantum phenomena) through socially co-constructed blends</cite>. <cite id="fa7920dc-2">Beyond creativity tools, blending is central to innovation processes, combining familiar domains to produce novel, sometimes patented effects, reflecting how theory change often emerges by stitching together known elements in new ways</cite>. <cite id="ada0e252-0">Mapping across frames and mental spaces (source/target) creates the blend where new meaning emerges; analogic, metaphorical, and categorial mappings are key operators</cite>.
- Mechanisms of theory transformation. <cite id="fa7920dc-1">The blend is not a mere sum of inputs but a structurally higher space formed by shared generic structure plus newly formed links, enabling richer explanatory hierarchies and multi-scope semantic networks</cite>. <cite id="ada0e252-4">Scientific creativity can be categorized into combinational (connecting within a paradigm), exploratory (deepening within), and transformational (transcending paradigms); Kuhn’s disciplinary matrices and Thagard’s conceptual systems capture how adoption of new ideas connects, expands, or revolutionizes conceptual space, with transformational creativity often driving conceptual revolutions</cite>.
- Case exemplars of reframing and reorganization. <cite id="b50dab97-1">A diachronic frame analysis of Austin’s shift from the constative/performative distinction to speech act theory illustrates how conceptual structures change and enrich, showing how reframing can reorganize explanatory concepts</cite>. <cite id="ada0e252-2">In late-20th-century Earth sciences, plate tectonics, impact theory for the K–T extinction, and Snowball Earth represent major conceptual advances that reorganize thinking to varying degrees; while not all match Kuhn’s strict paradigm incommensurability, they show that theory change can scale from partial reconceptualization to full reorganization</cite>.
- Biological and educational illustrations of blending-driven change. <cite id="fa7920dc-0">Students blending intuitive metaphors and expert concepts to understand quantum phenomena, and co-constructing integrated models via discussion, show how social blending scaffolds conceptual change</cite>. <cite id="fa7920dc-4">Neurocognitive evidence ties blending’s cross-domain integration to creativity and innovation, indicating brain-level mechanisms for generating novel scientific ideas by combining existing knowledge structures</cite>.

Conditions and trade-offs in blending-and-framing-driven theory change
- Productivity vs coherence. <cite id="fa7920dc-0">Unstructured blending can leave learners floundering without guidance, underscoring the need for scaffolding (e.g., anchoring to evidence, highlighting conceptual “hooks”) to focus mappings and avoid incoherent synthesis</cite>. <cite id="b50dab97-2">Framings can be strategically chosen to steer research agendas (e.g., funding priorities) by emphasizing certain mechanisms or outcomes, so governance and ethics of framing are essential to prevent myopic or normatively biased theory change</cite>.
- Comparative evaluation and progress. <cite id="ada0e252-2">Cohen emphasizes that judgments of “revolution” depend on stages of development, impact on educational materials, and expert evaluation; this provides criteria for assessing whether blended frames constitute genuine advances or merely rebranded puzzles</cite>. <cite id="b50dab97-3">Popper’s critique of the “myth of the framework” cautions against incommensurability that blocks criticism; this supports designing frames that remain mutually intelligible and evaluable, enabling cumulative progress</cite>.
- Scale and incommensurability. <cite id="ada0e252-2">Not all advances are full Kuhnian revolutions; some are partial reconceptualizations or expansions within a paradigm, while others may present deeper incommensurability and crisis</cite> <cite id="b50dab97-0">Frame analyses distinguish inter-conceptual vs intra-conceptual, structural vs content change, and enrichment, clarifying when shifts are compatible vs transformative</cite>.

Practical implications for research practice
- Framing techniques to shape inquiry. <cite id="b50dab97-2">Use domain-critical framings (e.g., mechanistic cascades, networked systems) to orient problem selection and hypothesis generation, making abstract phenomena tractable and guiding evidence search</cite> <cite id="b50dab97-4">Leverage frame technologies (slots/slots, matrices, visual graphs) to compress and systematize knowledge, fix analogies and generalizations, and track conceptual relations</cite>.
- Blending strategies to generate and test new theories. <cite id="ada0e252-0">Pre-specify mappings between input domains (source/target) via shared frames and cognitive models, and use co-referential anchors to construct blended spaces with testable implications</cite> <cite id="fa7920dc-0">Structure collaborative discussions to highlight cross-idea “hooks,” and scaffold students’/researchers’ ability to identify meaningful intersections, transforming disparate literatures into integrated models</cite>.

- In normal science, frames stabilize the disciplinary matrix; blending remains local—connecting anomalies to existing models or cross-pollinating subfields—producing exploratory or combinational creativity. <cite id="ada0e252-4">Exploratory creativity thrives within paradigms and is often “puzzle solving,” yet remains creative; combinational creativity connects elements across a paradigm but is difficult because no paradigm preposes such combinations</cite>. <cite id="fa7920dc-0">Educational and collaborative settings show how guided blending helps teams integrate concepts into coherent models</cite>.
- When anomalies and reframing pressures build, shifts to higher-level blends can reorganize theory. <cite id="fa7920dc-1">The integration of entry spaces yields new hierarchical structures and multi-scope networks that were not present before, enabling richer explanations</cite> <cite id="b50dab97-0">Conceptual enrichment allows growth without wholesale replacement; accommodation replaces or modifies structures when conflicts are intractable</cite>.
- Major revolutions occur when blended frames supply incommensurable but compellingly coherent new paradigms, altering problems, methods, and standards. <cite id="ada0e252-2">Kuhn’s account emphasizes incommensurability and crisis; alternatives like Cohen’s staged model stress individual genesis, publication, and community acceptance, both underscoring social-cognitive conditions for theory change</cite> <cite id="b50dab97-2">Domain cases like Alzheimer’s show how a cascade framing changes what counts as central evidence and acceptable interventions, illustrating how reframing can precipitate theory-level shifts</cite>.
- Across science and education, the same cognitive mechanisms apply: selecting frames, mapping across domains, anchoring blends to evidence, and iteratively testing and communicating the new theory space. <cite id="fa7920dc-4">Neurocognitive work supports blending as a general mechanism for creative insight generation</cite> <cite id="b50dab97-1">Applied frame analyses demonstrate how concepts are restructured over time into more powerful explanatory frameworks</cite>.

Practical checklist for a researcher
- Clarify your current frame: list core assumptions, concepts, and evaluative criteria. <cite id="b50dab97-0">Use frame structures (attribute–value) and graph formalizations to make implicit commitments explicit</cite>.
- Search for cross-domain blends: identify a source domain that clarifies puzzles, and enumerate candidate mappings. <cite id="ada0e252-0">Operationalize analogic, metaphorical, and categorial mappings with co-referential anchors</cite>.
- Build and test the blend: construct a provisional blended model; generate predictions and falsifiable implications; run small-scale tests (analogy-based cases, simulations). <cite id="fa7920dc-0">Scaffold collaborative integration to surface and connect diverse ideas into coherent blends</cite>.
- Evaluate change type and stage: assess whether you are in exploratory/combinational vs transformational territory; plan acceptance pathways. <cite id="ada0e252-4">Use paradigm/conceptual-systems diagnostics to anticipate barriers and strategies for uptake</cite>.
- Communicate with appropriate framing: choose frames that are commensurate with audiences and lay understandings where feasible; disclose strategic framings that may influence priorities. <cite id="b50dab97-3">Maintain a “view from somewhere” while enabling “view from nowhere” critical engagement across frames</cite> <cite id="b50dab97-2">Align scientific framings with societal discourses to ensure responsible translation</cite>.

Conclusion: Blending and framing as dual engines of theory change
- Semantic framing governs the lens through which phenomena are seen and compared; conceptual blending implements the synthesis that creates explanatory gains, reorganizes concepts, and, under sustained pressure, replaces paradigms. <cite id="b50dab97-0">Frames and frame analyses offer a rigorous basis for tracking conceptual and theoretical change across time</cite> <cite id="fa7920dc-1">Conceptual integration produces qualitatively new conceptual packages by unifying existing structures with newly formed links</cite> <cite id="ada0e252-2">Scientific revolutions vary in scale, from partial reconceptualization to full reorganization, reflecting the productivity and contestability of blended frames</cite>. Together, they provide a mechanistic, testable account of how research programs evolve, how interdisciplinary breakthroughs occur, and how communities adjudicate when a new frame has genuinely advanced understanding. <cite id="b50dab97-4">Frames are both methods and technologies for organizing and compressing knowledge, making them practical levers for guiding theory change in the research process</cite> <cite id="fa7920dc-4">Blending’s cross-domain integration taps creative cognitive mechanisms that underpin scientific innovation</cite>.

Snippet: The development of conceptual knowledge is not a linear progress, as learning progressions might tempt one to think, but a process in which complex knowledge structures are added to and altered. Conceptual change theory describes how newly acquired concepts interact with pre-existing concepts [43]. According to this theory, new concepts are either assimilated or accommodated into existing knowledge structures [43]. While assimilation means that a concept is added to existing structures without interfering with them, accommodation occurs when new concepts conflict with existing structures and replace or modify them [43]. In evolution learning, conceptual change can be difficult for students, as misconceptions that can work very well in everyday contexts might contradict evolutionary principles, and affective components such as personal beliefs can oppose conceptual change [12,44]. 

Knowledge integration theory is another way to describe the development of conceptual knowledge in learners. It describes different approaches students can take to integrate new concepts and ideas with already existing ideas, similar to conceptual change theory [24]. In opposition to conceptual change, though, knowledge integration also considers the possibility that students may not engage with and eventually integrate conflicting ideas, as they may find cognitive strategies to validate their existing, scientifically inaccurate ideas [24]. It stresses the idea that students hold a multitude of ideas, both scientifically accurate and inaccurate at the same time, and science education should focus not only on introducing new ideas that may remain isolated within students' knowledge networks, but rather focus on building connections between scientifically accurate ideas and enabling students to apply them to appropriate phenomena [24]. This approach can be used to design instruction promoting integrated knowledge networks, including tasks such as concept mapping, that encourage students to consider the connections they draw between concepts [45].

Title: Conceptual change and conceptual enrichment: a frame-based reconstruction of Austin’s theory of speech acts
Snippet: Originally, frames were developed in cognitive psychology (Barsalou, 1992;Barsalou & Hale, 1993). Very soon, the frame model found its way into the philosophy of science where it has been successfully used to investigate scientific concepts and conceptual change (Andersen et al., 1996(Andersen et al., , 2006;;Votsis & Schurz, 2012, 2014). It was specified and elaborated to analyze different types of scientific concepts (Kornmesser, 2017(Kornmesser, , 2018) ) and in addition to scientific concepts, to analyze scientific theories (Kornmesser & Schurz, 2020). Further, much effort was made to formalize frames by graph theory Synthese (2024) 203 :2 (Petersen, 2007;Kornmesser, 2016) and to develop an ontology for frames (Hommen, 2019(Hommen, , 2020)). 1  The starting point of the line of thought of this article is Andersen et al. (2006) who showed that frames are a powerful tool to analyze scientific concept shifts with respect to T. Kuhn's approach of scientific revolutions. In the following, it will be argued that the frame model provides the means for even more detailed analysis of conceptual change. To this end, I will develop and apply frame analyses of what I call the distinction between inter-and intra-conceptual change (Aim 1) as well as the distinction between conceptual structure change and conceptual content change (Aim 2). Further, I will introduce the notion of conceptual enrichment as opposed to conceptual change (Aim 3). I will point out some consequences of the conceptual changes introduced for the relation between scientific concepts 2 and theories. In order to apply and to exemplify the different kinds of concept change of Aims 1 to 3, I will provide a diachronic frame analysis from John Austin's constative/performativedistinction to the introduction of his speech act concepts and post-Austin approaches of performatives (Aim 4). Aim 5 is to show that the frame model is a highly useful tool to analyze scientific concepts and conceptual change due to the attribute-value structure of frames (see below) and the easily accessible graphical representation of conceptual structures. However, as we will see, the frame model is not yet fully developed.
</snippet>

In Sect. 2, I will analyze the basic idea of Austin's constative/performative-distinction. I will provide frame representations of conceptual changes of the concepts constative and performative in the Sects. 3 and 4. Section 5 contains a frame analysis of the starting point of Austin's speech act theory. In order to make it as comfortable as possible for the reader, I will not start out by introducing all definitions of frames and kinds of conceptual changes at once in the beginning of the article, but I will introduce them step by step as we go along. Framings-and metaphors in particular-may have such a normative impact because we use them to make sense of the world around us, as famously argued by Lakoff and Johnson (1980). By making an implicit comparison with a more familiar concept, the metaphor serves as a model for how the abstract concept can be understood (Lakoff & Johnson, 1980). Particularly in science, which often revolves around making sense of abstract phenomena, metaphorical framings are crucial for theory building and hypothesizing (Knudsen, 2003). Together, the results of these framing analyses will show whether the research understanding of AD is congruent with the use of the term in the lay literature. Title: Frames in the Social Sciences
Snippet: In a collection of addresses and lectures published at the end of his life, Sir Karl Popper provided a valuable guide to the elements of his philosophy of science [1]. The eponymous essay of the book deals with the myth of the framework: roughly, the idea that agents with different views and understandings cannot really communicate with each other. Their ways of thinking are incommensurable. According to Popper, such a position is flawed because it does away with the notion of objective truth and replaces it with a relative one, appropriate for each framework. This was a sort of anathema to Popper whose metaphysical conviction was one of objective truth, the same for everyone. Science is about rationality and critical discussion, and the latter can take place even among discussants with very different frames of reference. Thus, scientific knowledge and objectivity require a "view from nowhere" which is both description and position independent [2]. 

Regardless of this admonishment, during the last decades, the notion of frame has become one of the most influential concepts in several branches of social sciences and research. In the last half a century, the ideas of frame and framing have been applied in the most diverse disciplines and research areas, among which: sociology, cognitive sciences, psychology, political science, behavioral economics and linguistics, artificial intelligence, communication and media studies. Worth noting the notion of frame has been also applied outside social sciences, not only, as we shall briefly recall, in computer science, but also in mathematical sciences or electrical engineering. For instance, on frames theories in mathematics see [3]. 

In 2002, David Kahneman won the Nobel Prize in Economics exactly for having discovered the framing effects problem, i.e., what issues arise when the manner in which alternatives are presented matters for choice [4]. Since then, not only frames and framing have ceased to be unsound entities in scientific research, but they have been one of main tools in the building of relational social sciences [5]. 

Hence, the purpose of this paper is to provide a multi-disciplinary overview of existing notions of frame in social sciences. In doing this, we review main interpretations of the concept provided by different disciplines, and focus on their main knowledge spillovers for other fields of scientific inquiry.
</snippet>

Title: METHODOLOGICAL ASPECTS OF FRAME MODELLING AND STRUCTURAL FRAME ANALYSIS IN FOREIGN LANGUAGE TEACHING
Snippet: "Technology" is a system of conditions, forms, methods, means and criteria for solving a task". Based on the above, frame technology is understood as the study of educational material structured in a certain way in a specially organized sequence. The main feature of the technology is to increase the amount of knowledge learnt without increasing the teaching time. Usually a frame consists of several cells (slots), each of which has its own purpose. Thus, a frame is a model -an abstract image of standard stereotypical situations in symbols, a rigid construction containing as elements empty windows -slots, which are repeatedly recharged with information. With the help of the frame model, it is possible to compress structure and systematize information in the form of tables, matrices. Thus, in the practice of adapting frame theory to the educational sphere, a frame can be considered as a model, as a way/method and as a technology. The universal features of the frame from the standpoint of various scientific schools include: stereotyping; visualization capability; graphic form; availability of key characters, images, words; fixing analogies and generalizations. Stephan Kornmesser notes that "In the philosophy of science, the frame model is used in order to represent and analyze scientific concepts and conceptual change. However, the potential of the frame model is far from being fully exploited" [3: 228]. 

The frame approach has a long history, but it is difficult to speak about its unity. The phrases "frame theory" and "frame approach" can be found in the works of linguists, researchers of artificial intelligence, sociologists, psychologists (both cognitive and humanistic), political scientists, etc. Moreover, different researchers put different meanings into the word "frame" itself. In the light of the above, in our work the expressions "frame theory" and "frame approach" are different in meaning and are used accordingly. 

Frame theory is an expression of the frame approach in a particular science (linguistics, computer science, sociology, etc.). Developments within the frame approach found one of their first applications in the field of Artificial Intelligence (AI). Title: Open-Mouthed Wonder — an Account of Metonymy-Based Compound Epithets
Snippet: Speaking of conceptualization, two theories emerged within the domain of cognitive approaches -the Conceptual Metaphor Theory initiated by Lakoff and Johnson (1980) and the Theory of Mental Spaces which gave rise to the Theory of Conceptual Integration resulting from a joint venture by Fauconnier andTurner (1998, 2003). Lakoff and Johnson assumed that "…the locus of metaphor is not in language at all, but in the way we conceptualize one mental domain in the terms of another." (Lakoff 2006: 185). Based on their observations, Conceptual integration theory was initiated in early 1990s only to be summed up by its authors in a 2002 work titled The Way We Think. According to them, "Conceptual blending is a basic mental operation that leads to new meaning" (Fauconnier and Turner, 2003). In Fauconnier's words, the Theory is based on the notion of mental spaces: "small conceptual packets constructed as we think and talk for purposes of local understanding and action … partial assemblies containing elements … structured by frames and cognitive models" (Fauconnier 2006: 662). 

The role of domains from Conceptual Metaphor Theory was replaced by mental spaces in CIT. Still, these two notions do not represent counterparts -"...while domains (i.e. concepts, frames etc.) are stable and stored, mental spaces are transitory and ephemeral, and usually not memorized, though they can turn into stabilized semantic knowledge." (Kok, Bublitz 2011: 295). Unlike the Conceptual Metaphor Theory, CIT comprises of four mental spaces: two input spaces, generic space and the blend. The input spaces are similar to source and target domains as elements from both spaces are conceptually integrated. Generic space represents conceptual structure that is shared by both inputs and the blended space is where material from the two inputs combines and interacts. In the process, a mapping takes place in which an object or element in one mental space corresponds to an object or element in another. 

Figure 1. Schematic representation of conceptual blending (Fauconnier, 1997:51) As Fauconnier (1994) points out, mental spaces are related through co referential identity as well as analogic, metaphoric and categorial cognitive mapping.
</snippet>

Title: Geological Revolutions in the Late 20th and Early 21st Centuries: Plate Tectonics, Extraterrestrial Impacts, and Snowball Earth
Snippet: • Three major conceptual advances occurred in late 20th century Earth sciences; plate tectonics; an impact theory for the end-Cretaceous mass extinction; and the Snowball Earth hypothesis for late Neoproterozoic glaciations. 

• These examples differ in scale and thus in the extent to which they generated a reorganization of geological thinking. 

• These episodes do not match Kuhn's theory of paradigm shifts but instead suggest that Earth sciences advance by conceptual advances of varying magnitude. 

Kuhn viewed science, or at least physics, as governed by reigning conceptual paradigms within which science operates with an alternation between the problem-solving of normal science and the conceptual reformulation that occurs during a shift from one paradigm to a new one. These paradigms provide a conceptual structure for understanding a suite of scientific problems. 

Challenges and anomalies accumulate during the normal science phase, phenomena that cannot readily be explained under the existing paradigm. Eventually sufficient anomalies pile up that a crisis ensues, which is eventually resolved by a shift to a new paradigm. Crucially for Kuhn, paradigms are incommensurable. 

In his view, paradigm shifts reflect social and cultural pressures and are not strictly rational, so competing paradigms cannot easily be compared and evaluated against each other. This also means that paradigm shifts do not necessarily reflect progressive improvements towards some objectively more accurate depiction of the world. Thus, Kuhn rejected the views of most scientists that science approximates an accumulation of steadily more accurate view of the world. Of course, historians and philosophers of science have critiqued both Kuhn's representation and alternative epistemological formulations (see, e.g., debates over scientific realism). 

An alternative view of scientific revolutions was developed by Bernard Cohen in his Revolution in Science [ 9 ]. Cohen identifies four stages, beginning with initial conceptual change in an individual or small group and their commitment to systematically developing the idea and eventually publishing it. The fourth phase involves acceptance among the appropriate community. 

Cohen's criteria for judging whether changes represent intellectual revolutions are not independent but rest on evaluation of contemporaneous participants, the impact on textbooks, and evaluations by historians of science and scientists.
</snippet>

Title: Kuhn and conceptual change: on the analogy between conceptual changes in science and children
Snippet: Conceptual Change in School Science? 

We have argued that an analogy between Kuhn's and Piaget's notion of conceptual change seems to be misplaced. However, what about the more general analogy between Kuhn's notion of conceptual change and the kind of changes that may occur in school science (where the latter may be seen as a conceptual change from everyday to scientific conceptual schemes)? 

In order to be able to apply Kuhn's notions of 'conceptual change' and 'scientific revolution' to what happens in schools, CC needs to treat what children already know about the natural world as something akin to a scientific theory, since for Kuhn the change is between two comparable things. That is to say, in Kuhn's version of paradigm shifts within science, both the new and the old paradigm serve a similar purpose or aim (although the new paradigm may be more successful at certain aspects). Kuhn (1996, p.92) explicitly makes an analogy between political and scientific revolutions. In both the political and the scientific case, the change is between things that are comparable, i.e., that are the same kind of thing: on the one hand a form of government (e.g., a change from Monarchy to Democracy) or on the other a type of scientific theory (e.g., a change from Newtonian to Einsteinian physics). 

However, are pupils' 'naïve beliefs' sufficiently close to a scientific theory? In this section we will argue that they are not. Everyday understandings are not a 'conceptual scheme' in Kuhn's sense, since the latter refers to a systematic theory with interdefined terms (which is what his notion of incommensurability requires). In Kuhn's case, both the old and the new scientific theory serve the same kind of purpose (namely explaining aspects of the natural world in scientific terms) and can therefore be in competition: 

Like the choice between competing political institutions, that between competing paradigms proves to be a choice between incompatible modes of community life. (Kuhn 1996, p.94) In our view, common sense and science do not stand in this relation. In our society one can be, e.g., an accountant, a football player, a movie star, or an artist with or without knowledge of the latest scientific developments.
</snippet>

Title: Teaching scientific creativity through philosophy of science
Snippet: Paradigm theory provides a good infrastructure for teaching scientific creativity and more particularly, Boden's influential tripartite typology of creativity. This distinction between combinational, exploratory, and transformational creativity can be explicated in a scientific context through Kuhn's account of paradigms and Thagard's related notion of conceptual systems. Combinational creativity combines elements from different paradigms, exploratory creativity explores the space already set by the paradigm, and transformational creativity characterizes ideas that go beyond any known paradigm. Paradigm theory thus functions as a framework with which to categorize and analyze scientific creativity that can be taught by simply adding a perspective when teaching paradigm theory. The integration of paradigm theory and scientific creativity is of mutual benefit. Kuhn's disciplinary matrix and Thagard's conceptual systems provide, in different ways, structure to Boden's conceptual spaces. Moreover, Thagard's conceptual systems can capture what happens to the conceptual space when new creative ideas are adopted. This includes the conceptual revolutions induced by transformational creativity, the connection of distinct conceptual systems in combinational creativity, and the expansion of such systems through exploratory creativity. Exploratory creativity can also be informed by Kuhn's account of normal science, and a subdivision within transformational creativity is implicit in Kuhn's disciplinary matrix. The association between normal science and exploratory creativity in turn emphasizes that normal science -despite its description as "puzzle solving" -can be creative. This signifies, importantly, that scientific creativity is not limited to the big changes of scientific revolutions. Furthermore, the association between such scientific revolutions and a type of creativity that goes beyond a conceptual space can serve to emphasize that revolutions in science, as both Thagard and Kuhn point out, are often driven by conceptual changes. Finally, Boden's identification of a type of creativity that combines conceptual spaces suggests the possibility of combining paradigms, a notion that might be outright incomprehensible according to one reading of Kuhn. However, from Kuhn's account of normal science, we also get the qualification that combinational creativity in science is at least difficult -and probably more so than Boden indicates -since no paradigm will set such combination as one of its puzzles.
</snippet></tool_output><think>

Overview: Framing and blending as cognitive-epistemic engines of theory change
- Semantic framing shapes what is seen and how it is structured: it foregrounds certain features of a phenomenon, aligns concepts via analogy, and defines the community’s problem space and criteria of adequacy. Conceptual blending then drives theory change by integrating source/target domains or paradigms into a new blended space, producing novel predictions, models, and reorganizations of explanatory concepts. Together, framing selects and bounds the inputs; blending synthesizes them into richer or alternative theories. <cite id="b50dab97-0">Frames have been used to analyze scientific concepts and conceptual change with respect to Kuhn’s approach of scientific revolutions, enabling distinctions between inter-/intra-conceptual change, structural vs content change, and conceptual enrichment as opposed to change</cite> <cite id="fa7920dc-1">Conceptual integration theory posits that elements from two or more conceptual packages merge into a qualitatively new higher-level package (the blend) formed by shared structure (generic space) and emergent content</cite> <cite id="ada0e252-0">Cognitive blending integrates two input mental spaces via mapping across frames and cognitive models, yielding blended spaces where new meaning and insight emerge</cite>.

How semantic framing shapes the research process and theory change
- Problem selection and representation. <cite id="b50dab97-2">Framings (often metaphor-based) are crucial for theory building and hypothesizing in science; in Alzheimer’s disease, framings such as “cascade” shape the understanding of the disease and steer attention and evaluative norms, showing that the same phenomenon can be “understood” differently depending on how it is framed</cite>. <cite id="b50dab97-3">Across social sciences, “frame” and “framing” have become central for building relational sciences, with Popper arguing that frameworks need not be incommensurable in the strong sense that blocks rational communication, supporting the idea that shifts in frames can be critically discussed toward objective truth</cite>. <cite id="b50dab97-4">Frames provide stereotyped, visualized, and generalized structures that fix analogies and generalizations, and have been used to represent and analyze scientific concepts and conceptual change in philosophy of science</cite>.
- Integration and accommodation of anomalies. <cite id="b50dab97-0">Analyses of conceptual change distinguish assimilation (adding concepts without altering structure), accommodation (conflict leading to replacement/modification), and enrichment (adding content without changing structure), clarifying how reframing mediates whether anomalies prompt puzzle-solving or paradigm adjustment</cite> <cite id="fa7920dc-3">Conceptual change theory explains that new concepts may be assimilated or accommodated, with accommodation producing replacement or modification of existing structures</cite>.
- Evaluation and acceptability. <cite id="ada0e252-2">Alternative views of scientific revolutions (e.g., Cohen’s staged model) emphasize that change begins with individual conceptual advances and culminates in acceptance, with judgments depending on impact on textbooks and expert evaluation, linking reframing/blending products to social-cognitive criteria of theory acceptance</cite>.
- Interdisciplinarity and method. <cite id="b50dab97-0">Graph-theoretic formalization and ontology-building for frames show how structured representations can track conceptual relations and support systematic comparison over time, facilitating evidence-based reconstructions of theory change</cite>.

How conceptual blending shapes the research process and theory change
- Generative synthesis across domains. <cite id="fa7920dc-0">Conceptual blending enables learners and researchers to merge multiple ideas or analogies, creating integrated conceptual structures that support sensemaking in physics and cross-domain integration (e.g., math/physics, quantum phenomena) through socially co-constructed blends</cite>. <cite id="fa7920dc-2">Beyond creativity tools, blending is central to innovation processes, combining familiar domains to produce novel, sometimes patented effects, reflecting how theory change often emerges by stitching together known elements in new ways</cite>. <cite id="ada0e252-0">Mapping across frames and mental spaces (source/target) creates the blend where new meaning emerges; analogic, metaphorical, and categorial mappings are key operators</cite>.
- Mechanisms of theory transformation. <cite id="fa7920dc-1">The blend is not a mere sum of inputs but a structurally higher space formed by shared generic structure plus newly formed links, enabling richer explanatory hierarchies and multi-scope semantic networks</cite>. <cite id="ada0e252-4">Scientific creativity can be categorized into combinational (connecting within a paradigm), exploratory (deepening within), and transformational (transcending paradigms); Kuhn’s disciplinary matrices and Thagard’s conceptual systems capture how adoption of new ideas connects, expands, or revolutionizes conceptual space, with transformational creativity often driving conceptual revolutions</cite>.
- Case exemplars of reframing and reorganization. <cite id="b50dab97-1">A diachronic frame analysis of Austin’s shift from the constative/performative distinction to speech act theory illustrates how conceptual structures change and enrich, showing how reframing can reorganize explanatory concepts</cite>. <cite id="ada0e252-2">In late-20th-century Earth sciences, plate tectonics, impact theory for the K–T extinction, and Snowball Earth represent major conceptual advances that reorganize thinking to varying degrees; while not all match Kuhn’s strict paradigm incommensurability, they show that theory change can scale from partial reconceptualization to full reorganization</cite>.
- Biological and educational illustrations of blending-driven change. <cite id="fa7920dc-0">Students blending intuitive metaphors and expert concepts to understand quantum phenomena, and co-constructing integrated models via discussion, show how social blending scaffolds conceptual change</cite>. <cite id="fa7920dc-4">Neurocognitive evidence ties blending’s cross-domain integration to creativity and innovation, indicating brain-level mechanisms for generating novel scientific ideas by combining existing knowledge structures</cite>.

Conditions and trade-offs in blending-and-framing-driven theory change
- Productivity vs coherence. <cite id="fa7920dc-0">Unstructured blending can leave learners floundering without guidance, underscoring the need for scaffolding (e.g., anchoring to evidence, highlighting conceptual “hooks”) to focus mappings and avoid incoherent synthesis</cite>. <cite id="b50dab97-2">Framings can be strategically chosen to steer research agendas (e.g., funding priorities) by emphasizing certain mechanisms or outcomes, so governance and ethics of framing are essential to prevent myopic or normatively biased theory change</cite>.
- Comparative evaluation and progress. <cite id="ada0e252-2">Cohen emphasizes that judgments of “revolution” depend on stages of development, impact on educational materials, and expert evaluation; this provides criteria for assessing whether blended frames constitute genuine advances or merely rebranded puzzles</cite>. <cite id="b50dab97-3">Popper’s critique of the “myth of the framework” cautions against incommensurability that blocks criticism; this supports designing frames that remain mutually intelligible and evaluable, enabling cumulative progress</cite>.
- Scale and incommensurability. <cite id="ada0e252-2">Not all advances are full Kuhnian revolutions; some are partial reconceptualizations or expansions within a paradigm, while others may present deeper incommensurability and crisis</cite> <cite id="b50dab97-0">Frame analyses distinguish inter-conceptual vs intra-conceptual, structural vs content change, and enrichment, clarifying when shifts are compatible vs transformative</cite>.

Practical implications for research practice
- Framing techniques to shape inquiry. <cite id="b50dab97-2">Use domain-critical framings (e.g., mechanistic cascades, networked systems) to orient problem selection and hypothesis generation, making abstract phenomena tractable and guiding evidence search</cite> <cite id="b50dab97-4">Leverage frame technologies (slots/slots, matrices, visual graphs) to compress and systematize knowledge, fix analogies and generalizations, and track conceptual relations</cite>.
- Blending strategies to generate and test new theories. <cite id="ada0e252-0">Pre-specify mappings between input domains (source/target) via shared frames and cognitive models, and use co-referential anchors to construct blended spaces with testable implications</cite> <cite id="fa7920dc-0">Structure collaborative discussions to highlight cross-idea “hooks,” and scaffold students’/researchers’ ability to identify meaningful intersections, transforming disparate literatures into integrated models</cite>.
- Staged evaluation and communication. <cite id="ada0e252-4">Use paradigm-centric and conceptual-systems analyses to classify creativity as combinational vs exploratory vs transformational, and to plan acceptance pathways (textbook integration, community validation)</cite> <cite id="b50dab97-0">Track whether changes are assimilation (adding facts), accommodation (restructuring/replacement), or enrichment (adding content), and report these moves transparently to enable critique</cite>.
- Ethical and governance dimensions. <cite id="b50dab97-2">Audit framings for potential strategic steering (e.g., funding, media), and ensure that metaphorical framings do not occlude alternative mechanisms; align scientific framings with lay understandings where possible to reduce miscommunication</cite> <cite id="b50dab97-3">Design frames that remain commensurable with prior bodies of knowledge to preserve cumulative progress and enable rational debate</cite>.

Synthesis: how blending and framing move research from theory maintenance to transformation
- In normal science, frames stabilize the disciplinary matrix; blending remains local—connecting anomalies to existing models or cross-pollinating subfields—producing exploratory or combinational creativity. <cite id="ada0e252-4">Exploratory creativity thrives within paradigms and is often “puzzle solving,” yet remains creative; combinational creativity connects elements across a paradigm but is difficult because no paradigm preposes such combinations</cite>. <cite id="fa7920dc-0">Educational and collaborative settings show how guided blending helps teams integrate concepts into coherent models</cite>.
- When anomalies and reframing pressures build, shifts to higher-level blends can reorganize theory. <cite id="fa7920dc-1">The integration of entry spaces yields new hierarchical structures and multi-scope networks that were not present before, enabling richer explanations</cite> <cite id="b50dab97-0">Conceptual enrichment allows growth without wholesale replacement; accommodation replaces or modifies structures when conflicts are intractable</cite>.
- Major revolutions occur when blended frames supply incommensurable but compellingly coherent new paradigms, altering problems, methods, and standards. <cite id="ada0e252-2">Kuhn’s account emphasizes incommensurability and crisis; alternatives like Cohen’s staged model stress individual genesis, publication, and community acceptance, both underscoring social-cognitive conditions for theory change</cite> <cite id="b50dab97-2">Domain cases like Alzheimer’s show how a cascade framing changes what counts as central evidence and acceptable interventions, illustrating how reframing can precipitate theory-level shifts</cite>.
- Across science and education, the same cognitive mechanisms apply: selecting frames, mapping across domains, anchoring blends to evidence, and iteratively testing and communicating the new theory space. <cite id="fa7920dc-4">Neurocognitive work supports blending as a general mechanism for creative insight generation</cite> <cite id="b50dab97-1">Applied frame analyses demonstrate how concepts are restructured over time into more powerful explanatory frameworks</cite>.

Practical checklist for a researcher
- Clarify your current frame: list core assumptions, concepts, and evaluative criteria. <cite id="b50dab97-0">Use frame structures (attribute–value) and graph formalizations to make implicit commitments explicit</cite>.
- Search for cross-domain blends: identify a source domain that clarifies puzzles, and enumerate candidate mappings. <cite id="ada0e252-0">Operationalize analogic, metaphorical, and categorial mappings with co-referential anchors</cite>.
- Build and test the blend: construct a provisional blended model; generate predictions and falsifiable implications; run small-scale tests (analogy-based cases, simulations). <cite id="fa7920dc-0">Scaffold collaborative integration to surface and connect diverse ideas into coherent blends</cite>.
- Evaluate change type and stage: assess whether you are in exploratory/combinational vs transformational territory; plan acceptance pathways. <cite id="ada0e252-4">Use paradigm/conceptual-systems diagnostics to anticipate barriers and strategies for uptake</cite>.
- Communicate with appropriate framing: choose frames that are commensurate with audiences and lay understandings where feasible; disclose strategic framings that may influence priorities. <cite id="b50dab97-3">Maintain a “view from somewhere” while enabling “view from nowhere” critical engagement across frames</cite> <cite id="b50dab97-2">Align scientific framings with societal discourses to ensure responsible translation</cite>.

Conclusion: Blending and framing as dual engines of theory change
- Semantic framing governs the lens through which phenomena are seen and compared; conceptual blending implements the synthesis that creates explanatory gains, reorganizes concepts, and, under sustained pressure, replaces paradigms. <cite id="b50dab97-0">Frames and frame analyses offer a rigorous basis for tracking conceptual and theoretical change across time</cite> <cite id="fa7920dc-1">Conceptual integration produces qualitatively new conceptual packages by unifying existing structures with newly formed links</cite> <cite id="ada0e252-2">Scientific revolutions vary in scale, from partial reconceptualization to full reorganization, reflecting the productivity and contestability of blended frames</cite>. Together, they provide a mechanistic, testable account of how research programs evolve, how interdisciplinary breakthroughs occur, and how communities adjudicate when a new frame has genuinely advanced understanding. <cite id="b50dab97-4">Frames are both methods and technologies for organizing and compressing knowledge, making them practical levers for guiding theory change in the research process</cite> <cite id="fa7920dc-4">Blending’s cross-domain integration taps creative cognitive mechanisms that underpin scientific innovation</cite>.
</answer>

Title: GLITTER: An AI-assisted Platform for Material-Grounded Asynchronous Discussion in Flipped Learning
Snippet: In educational contexts, conceptual blending theory explains how learners generate novel insights by merging multiple ideas or analogies. For example, blending has supported student sensemaking in physics by enabling integrated conceptual structures [45], helped students creatively engage with complex scientific phenomena through intuitive metaphors [30], and facilitated students' integration of mathematics and physics concepts during problemsolving [20,32]. Additionally, blending has been observed in collaborative small-group learning, where students jointly construct integrated mental models through social interaction, deepening their conceptual understanding of challenging topics such as quantum mechanics [31]. Conceptual blending can enrich material-based discussions by offering a structured framework for integrating diverse perspectives with learning materials, helping learners connect their ideas with peers' contributions to foster innovative thinking. By structuring discussions around specific materials, blending can drive students to creatively synthesize diverse ideas grounded in evidence. However, using conceptual blending in this context also poses challenges. Students often struggle to identify meaningful conceptual intersections between their ideas without guidance. Effective scaffolding is therefore essential to help students discover these conceptual connections, providing enough structure to focus their reasoning while still encouraging creative exploration of potential conceptual blends. 

To address this, drawing on conceptual blending theory as its foundational framework, Glitter implements a Multi-framework Keyword Highlighting feature to visually suggest potential connections between posts and a Conceptual Blending with Anchoring Evidence feature to guide students in merging their ideas with those of peers. The system treats students' posts and peers' content as "input spaces", facilitating the discovery of novel relationships between seemingly disparate concepts and transforming them into integrated mental models.

Title: SEMANTIC EXTENSION OF “HUMAN COLORS” WHITE, PALE AND GRAY
Snippet: The two entry spaces are close and could be equated with the source and target domain in the conceptual metaphor theory. In the generic space, common elements of the two entry spaces are reflected, and the blend entails the unification process of entry spaces through which new content is formed. 

Conceptual integration theory assumes that elements of two or more conceptual packages merge (blend), creating a qualitatively new and structurally higher conceptual package (blending space). The new space (blend) is not a simple set of common elements of entry mental spaces. It is important for it to form a new, higher and more complex hierarchical structure, which occurs at the integration process. This refers to the basic fourfold model, but it is only the basic unit that continues to form links in networks of such models (semantic network). For example, Zoltan Koevecses (Zoltan Koevecses 2006: 276) notes a difference between the following: simplex networks, mirror networks, single-scope networks, double-scope networks and multi-scope networks. 

Unlike the conceptual metaphor theory, which is primarily a semantic theory, the conceptual integration theory aims to be a general theory of cognition, applicable to different domains. It is a theory that attempts to become a viable macrostructure, which could link cognitive science and explain the sense of human creativity (Antović, Tasić 2011: 1522). This specific theory is used in other scientific fields such as anthropology, theory of literature and many others.

Title: The dynamics of emergent entrepreneurship: a retrospective analysis of properties and possibilities for inference by conceptual blending of competencies and opportunities
Snippet: " 

Blending theory, also known as Conceptual Blending Theory (CBT) or Conceptual Integration, is now a cornerstone of modern cognitive linguistics with significant influence on cognitive science. Beyond traditional creativity tools like brainstorming, blending theory plays a central role in approaches involving assumptions, metaphors, and similar techniques, often essential in achieving innovations such as patents, which frequently combine two familiar domains to produce a novel and surprising effect. The theory also holds key implications for semantic theory (Oakley and Pascual 2017) and has become integral to cognitive modelling and computational creativity, particularly in advancing artificial intelligence (Falmer and Plaza 2019). In the popular literature Steven Johnson's book "Where good Ideas Come From" (Johnson, 2010) has created attention and practical impact based on essentially the basic principles of blending.

Title: Describing students’ learning about evolution through the lens of digital concept mapping
Snippet: The development of conceptual knowledge is not a linear progress, as learning progressions might tempt one to think, but a process in which complex knowledge structures are added to and altered. Conceptual change theory describes how newly acquired concepts interact with pre-existing concepts [43]. According to this theory, new concepts are either assimilated or accommodated into existing knowledge structures [43]. While assimilation means that a concept is added to existing structures without interfering with them, accommodation occurs when new concepts conflict with existing structures and replace or modify them [43]. In evolution learning, conceptual change can be difficult for students, as misconceptions that can work very well in everyday contexts might contradict evolutionary principles, and affective components such as personal beliefs can oppose conceptual change [12,44]. 

Knowledge integration theory is another way to describe the development of conceptual knowledge in learners. It describes different approaches students can take to integrate new concepts and ideas with already existing ideas, similar to conceptual change theory [24]. In opposition to conceptual change, though, knowledge integration also considers the possibility that students may not engage with and eventually integrate conflicting ideas, as they may find cognitive strategies to validate their existing, scientifically inaccurate ideas [24]. It stresses the idea that students hold a multitude of ideas, both scientifically accurate and inaccurate at the same time, and science education should focus not only on introducing new ideas that may remain isolated within students' knowledge networks, but rather focus on building connections between scientifically accurate ideas and enabling students to apply them to appropriate phenomena [24]. This approach can be used to design instruction promoting integrated knowledge networks, including tasks such as concept mapping, that encourage students to consider the connections they draw between concepts [45].

Title: The Neural Correlates of Creativity and Innovation in Various Domains and Contexts in Germany
Snippet: Originated by Gilles Fauconnier and Mark Turner, Conceptual Blending Theory posits that creativity arises from the process of blending different conceptual domains or mental spaces to create novel and meaningful ideas. This theory suggests that the human mind has the ability to integrate disparate concepts from various domains, resulting in innovative insights. In the context of the neural correlates of creativity and innovation, Conceptual Blending Theory is relevant as it provides a framework for understanding how the brain combines existing knowledge and experiences to generate novel ideas across different domains and contexts (Fauconnier & Turner, 1998).

The two entry spaces are close and could be equated with the source and target domain in the conceptual metaphor theory. In the generic space, common elements of the two entry spaces are reflected, and the blend entails the unification process of entry spaces through which new content is formed. 

Conceptual integration theory assumes that elements of two or more conceptual packages merge (blend), creating a qualitatively new and structurally higher conceptual package (blending space). The new space (blend) is not a simple set of common elements of entry mental spaces. It is important for it to form a new, higher and more complex hierarchical structure, which occurs at the integration process. This refers to the basic fourfold model, but it is only the basic unit that continues to form links in networks of such models (semantic network). For example, Zoltan Koevecses (Zoltan Koevecses 2006: 276) notes a difference between the following: simplex networks, mirror networks, single-scope networks, double-scope networks and multi-scope networks. 

Unlike the conceptual metaphor theory, which is primarily a semantic theory, the conceptual integration theory aims to be a general theory of cognition, applicable to different domains. It is a theory that attempts to become a viable macrostructure, which could link cognitive science and explain the sense of human creativity (Antović, Tasić 2011: 1522). This specific theory is used in other scientific fields such as anthropology, theory of literature and many others.

Blending theory, also known as Conceptual Blending Theory (CBT) or Conceptual Integration, is now a cornerstone of modern cognitive linguistics with significant influence on cognitive science. Beyond traditional creativity tools like brainstorming, blending theory plays a central role in approaches involving assumptions, metaphors, and similar techniques, often essential in achieving innovations such as patents, which frequently combine two familiar domains to produce a novel and surprising effect. The theory also holds key implications for semantic theory (Oakley and Pascual 2017) and has become integral to cognitive modelling and computational creativity, particularly in advancing artificial intelligence (Falmer and Plaza 2019). In the popular literature Steven Johnson's book "Where good Ideas Come From" (Johnson, 2010) has created attention and practical impact based on essentially the basic principles of blending.

snippet.text:
The development of conceptual knowledge is not a linear progress, as learning progressions might tempt one to think, but a process in which complex knowledge structures are added to and altered. Conceptual change theory describes how newly acquired concepts interact with pre-existing concepts [43]. According to this theory, new concepts are either assimilated or accommodated into existing knowledge structures [43]. While assimilation means that a concept is added to existing structures without interfering with them, accommodation occurs when new concepts conflict with existing structures and replace or modify them [43]. In evolution learning, conceptual change can be difficult for students, as misconceptions that can work very well in everyday contexts might contradict evolutionary principles, and affective components such as personal beliefs can oppose conceptual change [12,44]. 

Knowledge integration theory is another way to describe the development of conceptual knowledge in learners. It describes different approaches students can take to integrate new concepts and ideas with already existing ideas, similar to conceptual change theory [24]. In opposition to conceptual change, though, knowledge integration also considers the possibility that students may not engage with and eventually integrate conflicting ideas, as they may find cognitive strategies to validate their existing, scientifically inaccurate ideas [24]. It stresses the idea that students hold a multitude of ideas, both scientifically accurate and inaccurate at the same time, and science education should focus not only on introducing new ideas that may remain isolated within students' knowledge networks, but rather focus on building connections between scientifically accurate ideas and enabling students to apply them to appropriate phenomena [24]. This approach can be used to design instruction promoting integrated knowledge networks, including tasks such as concept mapping, that encourage students to consider the connections they draw between concepts [45].

snippet.text: Originated by Gilles Fauconnier and Mark Turner, Conceptual Blending Theory posits that creativity arises from the process of blending different conceptual domains or mental spaces to create novel and meaningful ideas. This theory suggests that the human mind has the ability to integrate disparate concepts from various domains, resulting in innovative insights. In the context of the neural correlates of creativity and innovation, Conceptual Blending Theory is relevant as it provides a framework for understanding how the brain combines existing knowledge and experiences to generate novel ideas across different domains and contexts (Fauconnier & Turner, 1998).

documents.title: GLITTER: An AI-assisted Platform for Material-Grounded Asynchronous Discussion in Flipped Learning
documents.snippet:
In educational contexts, conceptual blending theory explains how learners generate novel insights by merging multiple ideas or analogies. For example, blending has supported student sensemaking in physics by enabling integrated conceptual structures [45], helped students creatively engage with complex scientific phenomena through intuitive metaphors [30], and facilitated students' integration of mathematics and physics concepts during problemsolving [20,32]. Additionally, blending has been observed in collaborative small-group learning, where students jointly construct integrated mental models through social interaction, deepening their conceptual understanding of challenging topics such as quantum mechanics [31]. Conceptual blending can enrich material-based discussions by offering a structured framework for integrating diverse perspectives with learning materials, helping learners connect their ideas with peers' contributions to foster innovative thinking. By structuring discussions around specific materials, blending can drive students to creatively synthesize diverse ideas grounded in evidence. However, using conceptual blending in this context also poses challenges. Students often struggle to identify meaningful conceptual intersections between their ideas without guidance. Effective scaffolding is therefore essential to help students discover these conceptual connections, providing enough structure to focus their reasoning while still encouraging creative exploration of potential conceptual blends. 

To address this, drawing on conceptual blending theory as its foundational framework, Glitter implements a Multi-framework Keyword Highlighting feature to visually suggest potential connections between posts and a Conceptual Blending with Anchoring Evidence feature to guide students in merging their ideas with those of peers. The system treats students' posts and peers' content as "input spaces", facilitating the discovery of novel relationships between seemingly disparate concepts and transforming them into integrated mental models.

Title: Conceptual change and conceptual enrichment: a frame-based reconstruction of Austin’s theory of speech acts
Snippet: Originally, frames were developed in cognitive psychology (Barsalou, 1992;Barsalou & Hale, 1993). Very soon, the frame model found its way into the philosophy of science where it has been successfully used to investigate scientific concepts and conceptual change (Andersen et al., 1996(Andersen et al., , 2006;;Votsis & Schurz, 2012, 2014). It was specified and elaborated to analyze different types of scientific concepts (Kornmesser, 2017(Kornmesser, , 2018) ) and in addition to scientific concepts, to analyze scientific theories (Kornmesser & Schurz, 2020). Further, much effort was made to formalize frames by graph theory Synthese (2024) 203 :2 (Petersen, 2007;Kornmesser, 2016) and to develop an ontology for frames (Hommen, 2019(Hommen, , 2020)). 1  The starting point of the line of thought of this article is Andersen et al. (2006) who showed that frames are a powerful tool to analyze scientific concept shifts with respect to T. Kuhn's approach of scientific revolutions. In the following, it will be argued that the frame model provides the means for even more detailed analysis of conceptual change. To this end, I will develop and apply frame analyses of what I call the distinction between inter-and intra-conceptual change (Aim 1) as well as the distinction between conceptual structure change and conceptual content change (Aim 2). Further, I will introduce the notion of conceptual enrichment as opposed to conceptual change (Aim 3). I will point out some consequences of the conceptual changes introduced for the relation between scientific concepts 2 and theories. In order to apply and to exemplify the different kinds of concept change of Aims 1 to 3, I will provide a diachronic frame analysis from John Austin's constative/performativedistinction to the introduction of his speech act concepts and post-Austin approaches of performatives (Aim 4). Aim 5 is to show that the frame model is a highly useful tool to analyze scientific concepts and conceptual change due to the attribute-value structure of frames (see below) and the easily accessible graphical representation of conceptual structures. However, as we will see, the frame model is not yet fully developed.

Title: Conceptual change and conceptual enrichment: a frame-based reconstruction of Austin’s theory of speech acts
Snippet: However, as we will see, the frame model is not yet fully developed. Therefore, as part of Aim 5, I will improve the frame model where necessary throughout this investigation. 

The article is structured along the line of pursuing Aim 4-a diachronic analysis of the central concepts of Austin's investigation of how to act with language. In Sect. 2, I will analyze the basic idea of Austin's constative/performative-distinction. I will provide frame representations of conceptual changes of the concepts constative and performative in the Sects. 3 and 4. Section 5 contains a frame analysis of the starting point of Austin's speech act theory. In order to make it as comfortable as possible for the reader, I will not start out by introducing all definitions of frames and kinds of conceptual changes at once in the beginning of the article, but I will introduce them step by step as we go along. In the conclusions of Sect. 6, I will sum up the results. 

Just to be sure some final remarks on the program of the article: Please note that this article is dedicated to questions of scientific concepts and concept change within the philosophy of science and uses Austin's philosophy of language as an application of the notions introduced in the following. Throughout this article, I will reconstruct the most important of Austin's attempts to adequately determine the constative/performativedistinction. However, as is widely known, Austin himself dismisses his own attempts to determine this distinction and introduces his speech act theory. I will use the most important of Austin's conceptual developments to apply the notions of different kinds of conceptual change and of conceptual enrichment that I introduce in this article. That said, let's start accomplishing the aims. 

1 I just mentioned a few essential readings regarding the role of frames for the philosophy of science without claiming to be complete. Of course, frames have been used in other disciplines as well, such as linguistics and psychology as can be seen in the publications of the SFB991 The Structure of Representation in Language, Cognition, and Science (https://frames.phil.uni-duesseldorf.de). 2 I use the term "scientific concepts" in a wide sense also referring to concepts of the humanities.

Title: The Framing of “Alzheimer’s Disease”: Differences Between Scientific and Lay Literature and Their Ethical Implications
Snippet: For this reason, alarming framings of AD have also been used strategically to secure research funding (Fox, 2000). 

Framings-and metaphors in particular-may have such a normative impact because we use them to make sense of the world around us, as famously argued by Lakoff and Johnson (1980). By making an implicit comparison with a more familiar concept, the metaphor serves as a model for how the abstract concept can be understood (Lakoff & Johnson, 1980). Particularly in science, which often revolves around making sense of abstract phenomena, metaphorical framings are crucial for theory building and hypothesizing (Knudsen, 2003). Framings of AD as a cascade in science are therefore not mere rhetorical embellishments; they are not interchangeable with any other metaphor. Rather, they reflect how the author understands AD, namely as being like a cascade. In this article, we analyze the framings of AD applied in the international research literature and in Dutch national newspapers to retrieve the understandings of the term upheld in both literatures. Together, the results of these framing analyses will show whether the research understanding of AD is congruent with the use of the term in the lay literature. Second, by explicating the aspects of AD that are either emphasized or neglected by the employed framings, we analyze how the employed framings of AD steer the audiences' normative attitudes toward the disease. In the discussion, we further elaborate on the impact and consequences of our findings.

Title: Frames in the Social Sciences
Snippet: In a collection of addresses and lectures published at the end of his life, Sir Karl Popper provided a valuable guide to the elements of his philosophy of science [1]. The eponymous essay of the book deals with the myth of the framework: roughly, the idea that agents with different views and understandings cannot really communicate with each other. Their ways of thinking are incommensurable. According to Popper, such a position is flawed because it does away with the notion of objective truth and replaces it with a relative one, appropriate for each framework. This was a sort of anathema to Popper whose metaphysical conviction was one of objective truth, the same for everyone. Science is about rationality and critical discussion, and the latter can take place even among discussants with very different frames of reference. Thus, scientific knowledge and objectivity require a "view from nowhere" which is both description and position independent [2]. 

Regardless of this admonishment, during the last decades, the notion of frame has become one of the most influential concepts in several branches of social sciences and research. In the last half a century, the ideas of frame and framing have been applied in the most diverse disciplines and research areas, among which: sociology, cognitive sciences, psychology, political science, behavioral economics and linguistics, artificial intelligence, communication and media studies. Worth noting the notion of frame has been also applied outside social sciences, not only, as we shall briefly recall, in computer science, but also in mathematical sciences or electrical engineering. For instance, on frames theories in mathematics see [3]. 

In 2002, David Kahneman won the Nobel Prize in Economics exactly for having discovered the framing effects problem, i.e., what issues arise when the manner in which alternatives are presented matters for choice [4]. Since then, not only frames and framing have ceased to be unsound entities in scientific research, but they have been one of main tools in the building of relational social sciences [5]. 

Hence, the purpose of this paper is to provide a multi-disciplinary overview of existing notions of frame in social sciences. In doing this, we review main interpretations of the concept provided by different disciplines, and focus on their main knowledge spillovers for other fields of scientific inquiry.

Title: METHODOLOGICAL ASPECTS OF FRAME MODELLING AND STRUCTURAL FRAME ANALYSIS IN FOREIGN LANGUAGE TEACHING
Snippet: "Technology" is a system of conditions, forms, methods, means and criteria for solving a task". Based on the above, frame technology is understood as the study of educational material structured in a certain way in a specially organized sequence. The main feature of the technology is to increase the amount of knowledge learnt without increasing the teaching time. Usually a frame consists of several cells (slots), each of which has its own purpose. Thus, a frame is a model -an abstract image of standard stereotypical situations in symbols, a rigid construction containing as elements empty windows -slots, which are repeatedly recharged with information. With the help of the frame model, it is possible to compress structure and systematize information in the form of tables, matrices. Thus, in the practice of adapting frame theory to the educational sphere, a frame can be considered as a model, as a way/method and as a technology. The universal features of the frame from the standpoint of various scientific schools include: stereotyping; visualization capability; graphic form; availability of key characters, images, words; fixing analogies and generalizations. Stephan Kornmesser notes that "In the philosophy of science, the frame model is used in order to represent and analyze scientific concepts and conceptual change. However, the potential of the frame model is far from being fully exploited" [3: 228]. 

The frame approach has a long history, but it is difficult to speak about its unity. The phrases "frame theory" and "frame approach" can be found in the works of linguists, researchers of artificial intelligence, sociologists, psychologists (both cognitive and humanistic), political scientists, etc. Moreover, different researchers put different meanings into the word "frame" itself. In the light of the above, in our work the expressions "frame theory" and "frame approach" are different in meaning and are used accordingly. 

Frame theory is an expression of the frame approach in a particular science (linguistics, computer science, sociology, etc.). Developments within the frame approach found one of their first applications in the field of Artificial Intelligence (AI). To date, there have been many criticisms of these theories, also predominantly in the field of artificial intelligence.
